cards.formula: repeat: (a, b) = most frequent adjacent pair; replace every 'a b' with new token 'ab'; until |V| = target size (|V| = vocabulary size)
cards.example: Corpus 'low lower' starts as l o w _ l o w e r. The pair (l, o) occurs twice, so it is merged first into 'lo', giving lo w _ lo w e r.
cards.say: Byte pair encoding learns its vocabulary by counting. Start with single characters, find the pair that appears together most often, glue it into a new token, and repeat until the vocabulary is big enough.

items.l: l o w _ l o w e r
items.tip: Start: every character is its own token. The underscore marks the space.
Count how often each pair of neighbouring tokens appears in the whole corpus.
The pair l, o appears twice, the most of any pair, so it becomes the new token lo.

items.l: lo w _ lo w e r
items.tip: The corpus is rewritten with the new token.
Stop when the vocabulary hits the size you want. Weakness: a character never seen has no token.

beats.cap: Byte pair encoding started life as a compression trick, and it learns its pieces simply by counting.
Start with every letter on its own, then count which neighbouring pair shows up most often.
In low lower, the pair l and o appears twice, so it is glued into one new token.
Repeat until the list is big enough, and common chunks and whole words appear all by themselves.

cards.title: Byte-Level BPE and UTF-8
cards.text: How do you make sure no input is ever unknown? Run BPE on bytes instead of characters. UTF-8 stores every Unicode character as one to four bytes, and a byte can take only 256 values. So a base vocabulary of exactly 256 byte tokens can already spell out any valid text in any language, emoji included. Merges are then learned on top of the bytes, and the final vocabulary is the 256 bytes plus all merged tokens, each remembering which bytes it stands for. GPT-2 popularised this approach.
points: Works on UTF-8 bytes (values 0-255), not characters
UTF-8 uses 1-4 bytes per character
256 base tokens give complete coverage of any text
Final vocabulary = 256 bytes + learned merges
Each merged token stores its byte content for exact decoding
Popularised by GPT-2-style tokenizers
cards.formula: base vocabulary size = 256 (all byte values 0 to 255)
cards.example: 'Hi 🙂' -> bytes [72, 105, 32, 240, 159, 153, 130]: H, i and the space take 1 byte each, the emoji takes 4. In a Wikipedia paragraph about Obama, 'Barack' = 66 97 114 97 99 107, a space = 32 and '.' = 46.
cards.say: To never meet an unknown character, modern tokenizers start from raw bytes. Every character in UTF-8 is one to four bytes, and there are only two hundred fifty six byte values, so everything can be spelled.

items.tip: Any text in any language, emoji included.
Hi and the space take 1 byte each: 72, 105, 32. The emoji takes 4: 240, 159, 153, 130.
A byte has only 256 possible values, 0 to 255, so these base tokens can spell anything.
Merges are learned on top, each remembering exactly which bytes it stands for.
256 bytes plus all merged tokens. GPT-2 made this approach popular.

beats.cap: How do you make sure no character is ever unknown? You go one level deeper, down to raw bytes.
Every character is stored as one to four bytes, so Hi takes two bytes and a smiley takes four.
A byte has only two hundred fifty six possible values, so that many base tokens can spell anything.
Merges are then learned on top, and the final vocabulary is the bytes plus all those merges.

cards.title: Real Tokenizers in Action
cards.text: Production tokenizers behave much like the toy version, just with vocabularies learned from enormous corpora. OpenAI's online tokenizer shows that common English words usually become a single token, and the space in front of a word is typically glued onto it. The same sentence keeps six tokens for both GPT-4o and the newer GPT-5.x tokenizer, yet one ID changes: the final full stop. That small difference is a reminder that IDs belong to a specific tokenizer. A handy rule for English: one token is roughly four characters.
points: Common words are often a single token
The leading space is usually part of the word token
~4 English characters per token
100 tokens ≈ 75 words
Different model generations may assign different IDs to the same piece
cards.formula: tokens ≈ characters / 4; words ≈ 0.75 × tokens (English rule of thumb)
cards.example: 'Children go to the kindergarten.' -> 6 tokens. GPT-4o: [15295, 810, 316, 290, 92647, 13]. GPT-5.x and o1/o3: [15295, 810, 316, 290, 92647, 558]. Only the ID of the final '.' differs.
cards.say: Real tokenizers turn most common English words into a single token, usually including the space before them. As a rule of thumb, a token is about four characters, so a hundred tokens are roughly seventy five words.

items.tip: A common word: one token.
The space before the word is glued onto the token.
Same ID for GPT-4o and the newer GPT-5.x tokenizer.
Very frequent words get their own single token.
Even this longer word is a single token here.
GPT-4o uses ID 13, while GPT-5.x and o1 or o3 use ID 558. IDs belong to one tokenizer.

beats.cap: Let's peek inside a real tokenizer, the kind big chat models use every day.
Common English words usually become one token each, and the space in front sticks to the word.
Two model generations both give six tokens, yet the full stop gets a different number in each.
A handy rule: one token is about four characters, so a hundred tokens are roughly seventy five words.

cards.title: Special Tokens and Chat Templates
cards.text: Not every token stands for text. Vocabularies also reserve control tokens. A beginning-of-sequence token opens the input, an end-of-sequence token tells the model it is done and can stop generation, and a padding token fills up shorter sequences so a batch has equal lengths; padding is masked out of the loss and never predicted by decoder-only models. Chat models add role tokens that wrap the system instructions, the user's message and the assistant's reply into a chat template. The exact spelling differs from one model family to another.
points: <bos>: start of the sequence
<eos>: end of the sequence, can stop generation
<pad>: batch alignment only, masked and never predicted
<|system|>, <|user|>, <|assistant|>: role markers in chat templates
Formats are model-specific
cards.example: A chat turn might be stored as <|system|> You are helpful. <|user|> Hi! <|assistant|> Hello! <eos> (schematic; real templates vary by model).
cards.say: Some tokens are not words but signals. Start and end markers frame a sequence, padding fills gaps in a batch, and role tokens tell a chat model which part is the system, the user or the assistant.
covers: A2: Special tokens and chat templates

items.tip: Role tokens wrap the system instructions. Exact spelling differs by model family.
The user role marker tells the model who is speaking.
The end token says done and can stop generation. A start token opens the whole input.
Padding only fills shorter sequences in a batch. It is masked from the loss and never predicted.

beats.cap: Some tokens are not words at all, they are signals, like stage directions in a play script.
Role tokens tell a chat model which part is the system, which is the user, and which is itself.
An end token tells the model it is finished, while a start token opens the sequence.
Padding just fills gaps so a batch lines up, and it is ignored during training.

cards.title: Tokens Cost Context, Compute and Money
cards.text: Token counts quietly drive three practical budgets. First, the context window is measured in tokens, so a text that needs more tokens eats more of it. Second, every token is a position the model must process, so longer sequences mean more inference work and memory, with the exact growth depending on the architecture. Third, commercial APIs from providers such as OpenAI and Anthropic bill per input and per output token. Because tokenizers differ, comparing per-token prices alone is misleading; measure the cost on your own representative workload.
points: More tokens fill more of the context window
Token count sets the sequence length to compute on
Longer sequences raise inference work and memory
APIs bill input and output tokens separately
Per-token prices across models are not directly comparable
Benchmark cost on a representative workload
cards.formula: cost = n_input_tokens × price_in + n_output_tokens × price_out (prices usually quoted per 1M tokens)
cards.example: The same text needs 120 tokens with tokenizer A but 165 with tokenizer B, about 37% more. Even at an identical price per million tokens, model B costs more for that text. (Price tables compared: claude.com/pricing and openai.com/api/pricing, October 2025.)
cards.say: Tokens are the currency of language models. They fill the context window, they set how much computation is needed, and they are what you pay for. Since tokenizers differ, always compare costs on your real text.
covers: B2: Why tokenization matters in practice
A2: API pricing and tokenizer differences

items.tip: Same text, 120 tokens.
Same text, 165 tokens: about 37 percent more. Cost = input tokens x price in + output tokens x price out.

beats.cap: Tokens are the money of language models, quietly spending three budgets every time you use one.
They fill the context window, and every extra token is more work and memory for the model.
Providers bill per input and output token, but the same text can be 120 or 165 tokens.
So even at the same price per token, B costs more. Always test cost on your own real text.

cards.title: Tokenizer and Model Are a Pair
cards.text: Because the model only ever sees tokens, 'predict the next word' really means 'predict the next token'. The vocabulary size therefore fixes the width of the output layer: the model emits one score per vocabulary entry, and these scores can be turned into a probability distribution. It also means tokenizer and model are welded together during training. Swap in a different tokenizer and the same text maps to different IDs, so the model's learned knowledge no longer lines up; it must be adapted or retrained. Diagrams later often pretend one word equals one token, purely for readability.
points: Next-word prediction is really next-token prediction
Output (logit) dimension = vocabulary size V
Scores can be converted into probabilities
Tokenizer and model are a coupled system
Changing the tokenizer requires adaptation or retraining
Simplification ahead: one word = one token
cards.formula: z ∈ R^V: one logit per vocabulary entry, V = vocabulary size
cards.example: With a vocabulary of about 100,000 tokens, every forward pass ends in a vector of about 100,000 scores, one per possible next token.
cards.say: A tokenizer and its model are a matched pair. The model outputs one score for every token in the vocabulary, so swapping the tokenizer scrambles everything it learned and means retraining or adapting the model.
covers: B2: Engineering implications of the tokenizer

items.tip: Only this tokenizer's IDs make sense to this model.
One learned vector per vocabulary entry, tied to the tokenizer's numbering.
The learned knowledge lines up with these exact IDs.
Output size equals vocabulary size V. Scores can be turned into probabilities.

beats.cap: A tokenizer and its model are like a lock and its key, made for each other during training.
Predict the next word really means predict the next token, so the model scores every token in its list.
With about a hundred thousand tokens, every pass ends in about a hundred thousand scores.
Swap in a different tokenizer and the numbers no longer line up, so the model must be adapted or retrained.

lessons.title: Embeddings
lessons.goal: Understand how token IDs become learned vectors, how their geometry encodes meaning, and how cosine similarity compares them.

cards.title: IDs Are Labels, Not Meanings
cards.text: After tokenization a sentence is just a row of integers, and those integers are arbitrary. In 'The bank raised interest rates today', 'bank' happens to be 2317 and 'raised' 751, but that tells us nothing. ID 2317 is no closer in meaning to 2318 than to 57. If a network computed directly on these numbers, it would chase patterns that do not exist. The fix is an embedding: a lookup that swaps each ID for a learned continuous vector, placing tokens in a space where geometry can reflect meaning.
points: Token IDs are arbitrary indices
Numeric closeness of IDs means nothing
Each ID selects a learned vector instead
Vectors live in a continuous semantic space
Tokens are dictionary entries; embeddings express their meaning as geometry
cards.example: 'The bank raised interest rates today' -> [104, 2317, 751, 908, 432, 57] (illustrative). 2317 = 'bank', 751 = 'raised'; 2317 is not more similar to 2318 than to 57.
cards.say: Token IDs are just catalogue numbers. Two neighbouring IDs are not similar words. So instead of computing on the IDs themselves, we swap every ID for a learned vector, where distances can actually carry meaning.
covers: B2: Why token IDs are not enough
A3: Why token IDs need embeddings

scene.text: The bank raised interest rates today

items.tip: ID 104. Like a locker number: it says where to look, not what is inside.
ID 2317. Neighbouring ID 2318 could be any word at all - no shared meaning.
ID 751. Illustrative number; real IDs depend on the tokenizer.
ID 57. Bank, 2317, is no closer in meaning to 2318 than to this 57.

beats.cap: After tokenizing, your sentence about a bank raising rates is just a row of plain numbers.
Bank happens to be number 2317, but that is like a locker number, not a description.
Number 2317 is no more similar to 2318 than to 57, so doing maths on these numbers finds fake patterns.
So we swap every number for a learned list of values, a vector, where closeness can really mean something.

cards.title: The Embedding Matrix
cards.text: All token vectors live in one table, the embedding matrix E. It has one row per vocabulary entry, so V rows, and d_model columns. Embedding a token is literally copying the row whose index is its ID. Two numbers therefore shape the table: V sets how many vectors exist and also the size of the output vocabulary, while d_model sets how wide every vector is, and it is the same width the hidden representations keep through all Transformer layers. Wider means more capacity, but also more parameters and compute.
points: E has shape V × d_model, one row per token
Lookup at position t: copy row x_t
Vocabularies are often 100k+ tokens
d_model reaches roughly 10-16k in large models
d_model is also the hidden width of Transformer layers
Embedding parameters = V · d_model
cards.formula: E ∈ R^(V × d_model); e_t = E[x_t], where x_t is the token ID at position t and e_t its vector; number of embedding parameters = V · d_model
cards.example: V = 100,000 and d_model = 4,096 give 100,000 × 4,096 = 409,600,000, roughly 410 million parameters in the embedding table alone (illustrative). Each of the six tokens of 'The bank raised interest rates today' gets its own row.
cards.say: Every token's vector is stored as one row of a big table called the embedding matrix. Looking up a token just copies its row. With a hundred thousand tokens and four thousand dimensions, that table alone holds about four hundred million numbers.
covers: B2: Embedding matrix, lookup and parameter count

items.tip: Every vocabulary entry owns exactly one row of the table.
Rows are as wide as d_model, the same width used through all Transformer layers.
Real vocabularies often hold 100,000 or more tokens, so 100,000+ rows.
Embedding bank simply means copying row 2317. No maths, just a lookup.
Large models use widths of roughly 10,000 to 16,000 columns.
Parameters = rows x columns. 100,000 x 4,096 = 409,600,000, about 410 million.

beats.cap: Picture one giant spreadsheet where every token in the vocabulary gets its very own row.
To embed the word bank, you just find row 2317 and copy it out, nothing more.
The number of rows is the vocabulary size, and the width is how many numbers describe each token.
With a hundred thousand rows and four thousand columns, this table alone holds about four hundred ten million numbers.

cards.title: One-Hot Vectors vs. Embeddings
cards.text: Why not just use one-hot vectors? A one-hot vector is as long as the vocabulary and contains a single 1 at the token's position. It works, but badly: it is enormous and almost all zeros, every pair of one-hot vectors is orthogonal so no similarity can show up, and whatever the model learns about one token cannot transfer to another. An embedding layer fixes all three. Mathematically it is a linear projection: multiplying the one-hot vector by E picks out one row, compressing V dimensions into d_model learnable, shared ones.
points: One-hot: vocabulary-length vector with a single 1
Wasteful: huge and almost entirely zeros
All one-hot vectors are orthogonal: no relations
No generalization: each token learned from scratch
Embedding = linear projection of the one-hot vector
Compresses V dimensions down to d_model
cards.formula: e_t = E^T · x_t, where x_t is the one-hot vector of the token; the product simply selects row x_t of E
cards.example: Toy vocabulary of 6: [The, bank, raised, interest, rates, today]. 'bank' = [0, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0]; multiplying by E returns exactly the second row of E.
cards.say: A one hot vector is a giant list of zeros with a single one. It treats every word as equally unrelated. Multiplying it by the embedding matrix just picks one row, giving a compact vector that can be learned.
covers: A3: One-hot vectors and embeddings as projection

items.tip: As long as the vocabulary. Bank in a 6-word toy vocabulary: 0, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0.
All one-hot vectors are orthogonal, so no similarity can ever show up.
What the model learns about one token cannot transfer to another.
Compresses V dimensions down to d_model learnable numbers.
Related tokens can get nearby vectors.
One-hot times the matrix E is a linear projection that returns exactly one row of E.

beats.cap: Why not just mark each word with a giant list of zeros and a single one, like a light switch?
That one-hot list is enormous, treats every pair of words as totally unrelated, and shares nothing between words.
An embedding is short and dense, so related words can sit close and lessons can be shared.
Fun fact: multiplying the one-hot list by the embedding table simply picks out that word's row.

cards.title: Meaning Emerges as Geometry
cards.text: Nobody writes the embedding values by hand. E is a trainable parameter: its rows start random and are nudged by gradient updates together with every other weight in the LLM, driven by the training objective. Meaning ends up stored not in single numbers but in distances and directions. Tokens that appear in similar contexts drift toward similar positions, and regularities such as gender, tense or grammar can show up as roughly parallel offset directions, so simple vector arithmetic sometimes lands near the expected word.
points: E is trained jointly with all other parameters
Rows start random, updated by backpropagation
Meaning lives in distances and directions
Similar contexts -> similar vectors
Gender (king-queen, man-woman), tense (walk-walked), syntax (is-was, do-did) as directions
Relations can appear as linear offsets
cards.formula: king - man + woman ≈ queen (an analogy expressed as vector arithmetic)
cards.example: In a made-up 2D picture, the arrow from 'man' to 'woman' is parallel to the arrow from 'king' to 'queen'; both encode the same gender shift.
cards.say: The embedding table starts as random noise and is shaped by training. Words used in similar ways end up close together, and relationships like male to female or present to past can appear as consistent directions.

items.tip: Made-up 2D picture. Real embeddings have thousands of dimensions.
The step from man to woman is a gender direction.
King minus man plus woman lands near queen.
The arrow king to queen runs parallel to man to woman.
Tense can be a direction too: walk to walked, like is to was or do to did.

beats.cap: Nobody types these vectors in by hand; they start as random noise and get nudged during training.
Words used in similar sentences slowly drift toward similar spots, like friends who sit together.
Look: the step from man to woman matches the step from king to queen, the same gender shift.
So king minus man plus woman lands near queen, and meaning lives in distances and directions.

cards.title: Length Says Frequency, Direction Says Meaning
cards.text: Trained embedding spaces hide a surprising pattern. How often a word appears in the training data correlates with the length, or norm, of its vector. Very frequent words such as 'the', 'and' or 'of' receive many gradient updates, end up with larger norms, and point in similar directions, forming a dense cluster around the centroid of all embeddings, not around the origin. That cluster reflects generic usage rather than meaning. Rare words like 'neutrino' get smaller norms but distinctive directions out on the sparse periphery.
points: Word frequency correlates with vector norm
Frequent words: larger norms, more gradient updates
They cluster densely near the centroid (not the origin)
That cluster reflects generic usage, not meaning
Rare words: smaller norms, distinctive directions at the periphery
Rule of thumb: length ≈ frequency, direction ≈ meaning
cards.formula: ||e|| = sqrt(sum over k of e_k^2): the L2 norm (length) of embedding vector e
cards.example: Frequent: 'the', 'and', 'of' -> long, similar arrows near the centroid. Rare: 'cryptocurrency', 'neutrino' -> shorter arrows pointing in their own directions.
cards.say: Here is a neat pattern. Common words like the and of get long vectors that all point roughly the same way. Rare words get shorter but more distinctive directions. Length tracks frequency, direction tracks meaning.
covers: A3: Vector norm vs. direction (frequency effects)

items.tip: Very frequent: gets many gradient updates and a long vector.
Frequent words point in similar directions and crowd together.
They cluster near the centroid of all embeddings, not the origin.
Rare word: shorter vector, but its own distinctive direction.
Rare words live out on the sparse edges of the space.

beats.cap: Here is a neat secret hidden in trained embeddings: how long an arrow is tracks how common the word is.
Everyday words like the, and, of get lots of practice, grow long, and huddle in one crowded corner.
That crowd reflects generic usage, not real meaning, and sits around the average of all words, not the centre.
Rare words like neutrino get shorter arrows, but point in their own special directions.

cards.title: Cosine Similarity
cards.text: If direction carries meaning and length is mostly noise, compare vectors by their angle. Cosine similarity divides the dot product of two vectors by the product of their lengths, so scaling a vector changes nothing. The result lies between -1 and +1: +1 means the same direction, 0 means orthogonal and unrelated, -1 means opposite. Cosine distance is one minus the similarity. A helpful picture: normalise every embedding to length one, and all tokens become points on a high-dimensional sphere where the angle is the semantic distance.
points: Measures the angle between two vectors
Ignores vector length
+1 same direction, 0 unrelated, -1 opposite
Cosine distance = 1 - cosine similarity
Normalised embeddings are points on a hypersphere
cards.formula: cos_sim(e_i, e_j) = (e_i · e_j) / (||e_i|| · ||e_j||), with e_i, e_j vectors of length d_model; d_cos = 1 - cos_sim
cards.example: bank-loan 0.82 (strongly related), bank-interest 0.76 (related), bank-river 0.48 (moderate, the other meaning of bank), bank-banana 0.05 (unrelated); good-bad -0.62, increase-decrease -0.45, up-down -0.71, love-hate -0.58 (opposites). Synonyms like car-automobile approach +1.
cards.say: To compare two word vectors, we look at the angle between them, not their length. Pointing the same way gives one, unrelated gives zero, opposite gives minus one. Bank and loan score high, bank and banana almost zero.

items.tip: Our reference word. Cosine only cares about the angle, so stretching an arrow changes nothing.
bank-loan 0.82: strongly related. bank-interest is 0.76.
bank-river 0.48: moderate, thanks to the riverside meaning of bank.
bank-banana 0.05: about a right angle, unrelated.
Synonyms like car and automobile approach +1.
good-bad -0.62. Also up-down -0.71, love-hate -0.58. Cosine distance = 1 minus similarity.

beats.cap: If direction carries meaning, the fair way to compare two words is the angle between their arrows.
Bank and loan point almost the same way, scoring about point eight two, so they are strongly related.
Bank and river score a moderate point four eight, while bank and banana sit near zero, totally unrelated.
Opposites like good and bad point away, near minus one, so scores run from minus one to plus one.

cards.title: Word2Vec: Learning from Neighbours
cards.text: Long before LLMs, Word2Vec showed that useful embeddings can be learned from context alone. Its skip-gram variant is a shallow network: the one-hot vector of a centre word goes in, a hidden layer projects it to a small vector, and a softmax output predicts which words appear in a window around it. Training raises the probability of the real neighbours. Because words with similar neighbours must make similar predictions, their hidden vectors become similar, and those hidden weights are the embeddings. You can explore such spaces at projector.tensorflow.org.
points: Skip-gram: predict context words from a centre word
Shallow net: one-hot input -> hidden layer -> softmax
Training data: (centre, context) pairs inside a window
Maximise the probability of true context words
Hidden-layer weights become the word embeddings
cards.formula: maximise the sum of log p(context word | centre word), with p computed by a softmax over the vocabulary
cards.example: In 'The bank raised interest rates today' with centre word 'interest', the training pairs are (interest -> bank), (interest -> raised), (interest -> rates), (interest -> today).
cards.say: Word2Vec learns word vectors with a simple game: given a word, guess its neighbours. Words that share neighbours are forced toward similar vectors, and those learned weights become the embeddings.

items.tip: Input is the one-hot vector of the centre word.
A small projection. After training, these hidden weights are the word embeddings.
Softmax over the vocabulary. Pairs: interest to bank, raised, rates, today.

beats.cap: Long before chatbots, a tiny network called Word2Vec learned word meaning with a simple guessing game.
Feed in the word interest, squeeze it through a small hidden layer, then guess its neighbours.
Training rewards guessing the real neighbours: bank, raised, rates and today.
Words with similar neighbours must make similar guesses, so their hidden vectors become similar, and those are the embeddings.

cards.title: One Vector per Token, Whatever the Context
cards.text: There is one big limitation. The embedding lookup ignores neighbouring words entirely: the same ID always fetches the same row. So 'bank' gets an identical starting vector in 'The bank raised interest rates' and in 'They sat on the river bank', even though the meanings differ. Its static vector is a blend of all its uses, which is why bank-river scores a moderate 0.48. Separating finance from riverside meaning requires looking at the whole sentence, and that is exactly what attention in the following Transformer layers does.
points: Lookup is independent of surrounding tokens
Same token ID -> same initial embedding
Ambiguous words get one blended vector
Contextual meaning emerges in later layers
Motivates attention and the Transformer (Chapter 3)
cards.example: Matrix rows such as ID 0 -> [0.12, -0.08, ..., 0.44], ID 1 -> [-0.31, 0.17, ..., -0.06], ID 2317 -> [-0.09, 0.52, ...] with d_model e.g. 4096. Both 'bank' sentences fetch row 2317 unchanged.
cards.say: An embedding lookup is blind to context. The word bank gets the very same vector whether we talk about money or a river. Telling those meanings apart is the job of attention, which comes next.

items.tip: Here bank means a financial institution.
Lookup copies row 2317, a vector of 4096 numbers, unchanged.
Here bank means a riverside.
Exactly the same row. The static vector is a blend of all uses, so bank-river is only 0.48.

beats.cap: Imagine a dictionary that gives one definition per word, no matter which sentence you read it in.
In a money sentence, bank fetches row 2317 from the table.
Sitting on a river bank fetches the exact same row, because the lookup never looks at the neighbours.
Telling money from riverside needs the whole sentence, and that is the job of attention, coming next.

lessons.title: From Logits Back to Text
lessons.goal: Follow how the model's scores become probabilities, a chosen token and finally text, how the generation loop runs inside a context window, and how the same pipeline is trained.

cards.title: Logits: A Score for Every Token
cards.text: Once the input vectors have flowed through the LLM, the last position produces logits: one raw, unnormalised score for every entry in the vocabulary. With a 100,000-token vocabulary that is a vector of 100,000 numbers. Higher means the model finds that token more plausible as the continuation, but the values are not probabilities yet and can be negative or larger than one. A decoding strategy then reads these scores and commits to one token ID. Crucially, a causal LLM makes exactly one such next-token decision per forward pass.
points: Logits = raw, unnormalised scores
One logit per vocabulary entry
Higher score = more plausible next token
A decoding strategy (Chapter 5) picks the token
One forward pass = one next-token decision
cards.formula: z = (z_0, ..., z_(V-1)) ∈ R^V, one score per vocabulary token, V = vocabulary size
cards.example: After 'The capital of France is': ' Paris' (ID 12345) logit 8.4, ' Lyon' (6592) 3.1, ' France' (156) 2.7, ' London' (398) 1.9 (illustrative).
cards.say: At the end of each pass the model produces a raw score, called a logit, for every token it knows. For the capital of France prompt, Paris gets by far the highest score, but nothing is chosen yet.

items.tip: Token ID 12345. Highest score: the model likes this continuation most.
Token ID 6592. Plausible city, much lower score.
Token ID 156. Grammatical but odd here.
Token ID 398. Logits can even be negative - they are raw scores, not chances.

beats.cap: You type: the capital of France is. What should come next? The model has to decide.
It gives every single word it knows a raw score, called a logit. Paris gets a big one.
Lyon, France and London get scores too. In a real model that is a hundred thousand scores at once.
These are just scores, not chances yet. And each pass through the model makes exactly one next-word decision.

cards.title: Softmax: Scores to Probabilities
cards.text: To compare logits as chances, they are passed through softmax. Each score is exponentiated, which makes every value positive and stretches the gaps, and then divided by the sum of all exponentials, so the results lie between zero and one and add up to exactly one. The model's output is thus a probability distribution over the whole vocabulary. Softmax keeps the ranking of the logits, so the top score stays the top probability, but a gap of a few points in logits becomes a huge gap in probability.
points: Exponentiate, then normalise by the sum
Outputs are in (0, 1) and sum to 1
Gives a probability distribution over the vocabulary
Preserves the order of the logits
Small logit gaps become large probability gaps
Basis for greedy decoding, sampling and temperature
cards.formula: p_i = exp(z_i) / sum over j of exp(z_j), where z_i is the logit of token i and p_i its probability
cards.example: If only the four candidates above existed: exp(8.4) ≈ 4447, exp(3.1) ≈ 22.2, exp(2.7) ≈ 14.9, exp(1.9) ≈ 6.7; sum ≈ 4491. So P(' Paris') ≈ 0.990, P(' Lyon') ≈ 0.005, P(' France') ≈ 0.003, P(' London') ≈ 0.0015.
cards.say: Softmax turns raw scores into probabilities. It exponentiates every score and divides by the total, so everything is positive and adds up to one. A lead of five points makes Paris about ninety nine percent likely.

items.tip: exp(8.4) is about 4447, divided by the total of about 4491: roughly 99 percent.
exp(3.1) is about 22: roughly 0.5 percent.
exp(2.7) is about 15: roughly 0.3 percent.
exp(1.9) is about 6.7: roughly 0.15 percent.

beats.cap: Scores are hard to compare. We want chances that add up to one hundred percent. That is what softmax does.
Softmax makes every score positive and stretches the gaps, then shares out one hundred percent between them.
A gap of five points in score turns into ninety nine percent versus half a percent. The order never changes.
Now your turn: drag the temperature. Low makes the model confident, high spreads the chances out.

cards.title: The Generation Loop and When It Stops
cards.text: Generating an answer is a loop of four moves: process the current sequence, select the next token, append it, repeat. Each new prediction is conditioned on every token so far, including the ones the model just produced. Starting from 'The capital of France is', the loop adds ' Paris', then '.', then the end-of-sequence token. That last token is one way to stop. The application can also cap the number of generated tokens, or watch for other criteria such as a user-defined stop sequence. A high logit alone never stops generation.
points: Loop: process -> select -> append -> repeat
Each step adds exactly one token
Each step conditions on all previous tokens
Stop on <eos>
Stop at a configured generation limit
Stop on other criteria, e.g. stop sequences
cards.formula: x_(t+1) = select(LLM(x_1, ..., x_t)): the next token is chosen from the model's scores for the sequence so far
cards.example: 'The capital of France is' -> ' Paris' -> '.' -> <eos> (stop). A second illustration: 'The' -> 'cat' -> 'sat' -> 'on' -> 'the' -> 'mat'.
cards.say: Generation is a loop: run the model, pick a token, append it, and run again. It ends when the model emits an end of sequence token, when a length limit is reached, or when some other stop rule fires.

items.tip: The model processes the whole current sequence, including its own earlier outputs.
A decoding strategy chooses one token from the probabilities.
The new token is added to the end of the sequence.
Stops on the end-of-sequence token, a length limit, or a stop sequence. A high score alone never stops it.

beats.cap: Writing an answer is a loop, like a typist who looks at the page before every single key press.
Read everything so far, pick one token, add it to the end, and go around again.
The capital of France is, then Paris, then a full stop, then a special end token.
It stops on that end token, at a length limit, or on a stop phrase you choose.

cards.title: The Context Window
cards.text: The current context is the prompt plus everything generated so far, so it grows by one token every step. The context window is the maximum number of tokens the model can process at once; it acts like short-term memory, and each prediction only sees what is inside it. The length is fixed by the model design, and both prompt and output share it, so a longer prompt leaves less room to answer. At the limit, the application must stop, drop old tokens, summarise them or move knowledge into retrieval. Larger windows cost latency, memory and money.
points: Current context = prompt tokens + generated tokens
Window = max tokens processed in one step
Acts as the model's short-term memory
Fixed by the architecture; prompt and output share it
At the limit: stop, drop, summarise or retrieve (RAG)
Bigger windows -> more latency, memory and cost
cards.formula: n_prompt + n_generated <= L, where L is the context window length in tokens
cards.example: 'The capital of France is' = 5 tokens; after one step plus ' Paris' = 6 tokens (illustrative). Window sizes grew fast: GPT-1 512, GPT-2 1,024, GPT-3 2,048, GPT-4 32,768 tokens.
cards.say: The context window is the model's short term memory, measured in tokens. Your prompt and the answer share it. GPT one could hold five hundred twelve tokens, GPT four up to about thirty two thousand.
covers: B2: Growing context and the context window

items.tip: Your prompt tokens fill the window first.
Every generated token is added to the context.
The context grows by one token per step.
At the limit: stop, drop old tokens, summarise, or move knowledge into retrieval.

beats.cap: Think of the context window as the model's short-term memory, a desk with room for only so many tokens.
Your prompt goes on the desk first. Every new answer token takes one more spot.
Prompt and answer share the same desk, so a very long prompt leaves less room to reply.
Windows grew from about five hundred tokens in early models to tens of thousands, but bigger costs time and memory.

cards.title: Walkthrough: A 5-Token Window
cards.text: Let's run the whole pipeline by hand with a tiny context window of just five tokens. The prompt '<bos> The' is tokenized and placed in the window. The LLM predicts an ID, the detokenizer reveals its word, and the ID is pushed into the window for the next round. After four steps the window is full, so the oldest token, <bos>, slides out to make room. On the sixth step the model predicts the end-of-sequence ID and generation stops, leaving a complete little sentence.
points: Tokenizer -> IDs in the window -> LLM -> predicted ID -> detokenizer
Every predicted ID is pushed into the window
Window length 5 in this example
When full, the oldest token is dropped
Generation ends when <eos> (ID 513) is predicted
cards.example: IDs: The=464, cat=58624, sat=963, on=162, the=27, mat=7598, <eos>=513. Step 1: [<bos>, 464] -> 58624 'cat'. Steps 2-4: -> 963 'sat', 162 'on', 27 'the'. Step 5: window full, <bos> removed -> 7598 'mat'. Step 6: [58624, 963, 162, 27, 7598] -> 513 <eos>. Output: 'The cat sat on the mat'.
cards.say: Let's step through it with a window of only five tokens. Each predicted word is pushed in. When the window is full, the oldest token drops out. When the model predicts the end token, we stop with: the cat sat on the mat.

scene.text: The cat sat on the mat

items.tip: Starts after the begin token. Window: begin, The.
Step 1 predicts ID 58624, the detokenizer shows cat.
Step 2: ID 963.
Step 3: ID 162.
Step 4: ID 27. Now the five-slot window is full.
Step 5: the oldest token slides out to make room. Then step 6 predicts end-of-sequence, ID 513.

beats.cap: Let's run the whole machine by hand, with a tiny memory of just five tokens.
Each round the model predicts one ID, we turn it back into a word, and push it into the window.
After four rounds the window is full, so the oldest token slides out to make room.
Then the model predicts the end token and stops. We got a complete little sentence.

cards.title: Detokenization: IDs Back to Text
cards.text: The final station converts generated IDs back into readable text, and it must use exactly the same tokenizer configuration as encoding. For a byte-level tokenizer, each ID maps to its stored byte sequence; the bytes are concatenated and decoded as UTF-8, which correctly reassembles multi-byte characters such as emoji split across tokens. Because token boundaries are not word boundaries, you cannot just join token strings with spaces; leading spaces live inside the tokens. Merges are deterministic, so the round trip is lossless. Special tokens like <eos> end generation rather than appearing as text.
points: Inverse of tokenization: IDs -> tokens -> text
Same tokenizer configuration for encoding and decoding
Byte-level: IDs -> bytes -> concatenate -> UTF-8 decode
Token boundaries ≠ word boundaries; no naive space-joining
Deterministic merges make it lossless
<eos> ends generation instead of producing text
cards.formula: decode(encode(text)) = text (lossless round trip)
cards.example: [313, 3666, 25] -> [Hello, _world, !] -> 'Hello world!'. Generated IDs [12345, 13] -> ' Paris.'; then <eos> ends generation.
cards.say: Detokenization runs the tokenizer backwards. Each ID turns back into its bytes, the bytes are joined and decoded into characters. Spaces already live inside the tokens, so you never just glue tokens together with spaces.

items.tip: What the model actually produces: numbers.
Same tokenizer as for encoding - every ID maps to its stored bytes.
Spaces live inside tokens, so you never just glue words with spaces.
Rebuilds characters, even an emoji that was split across two tokens.
Lossless: decoding what you encoded gives back exactly the same text.

beats.cap: The model only speaks numbers. Detokenization is the translator that turns them back into text.
Each ID is looked up with the very same tokenizer, giving its little piece of bytes.
The bytes are joined and decoded, which even puts a split emoji back together.
Nothing is lost on the round trip, and the special end token simply stops the text.

cards.title: The Same Pipeline Learns
cards.text: Training reuses the exact same pipeline, just with the answer known in advance. Take 'The cat sat on the mat': the input is the sentence and the target is the same sentence shifted one token to the left, so every position must predict its successor. In the forward pass the model outputs a probability distribution over the vocabulary at each position. Cross-entropy compares it with a one-hot vector marking the correct next token, which boils down to minus the log probability of that token. Backpropagation then adjusts the weights so the right token becomes more likely.
points: Target = input shifted by one position
Forward pass: distribution over the vocabulary at every position
Cross-entropy loss vs. a one-hot target
Backpropagation computes gradients and updates weights
Every position gives a training signal at once
cards.formula: Loss = - sum over t of log p(x_(t+1) | x_1, ..., x_t); with a one-hot target, each term is minus the log probability of the correct token
cards.example: Input: 'The cat sat on the' -> Target: 'cat sat on the mat'. If p('cat' | 'The') = 0.5, that position's loss is -ln 0.5 ≈ 0.69; raising it to 0.9 lowers the loss to about 0.11.
cards.say: Training uses the same pipeline. The target is just the input shifted by one word. The model's probabilities are compared with the correct next token using cross entropy, and backpropagation nudges the weights to do better next time.

items.tip: Position 1 sees: The
If the model gives cat 50 percent, the loss here is about 0.69.
Position 2 sees: The cat
Every position is a small exam at the same time.
The last position sees everything before it.
Raising the chance of the right word to 90 percent drops the loss to about 0.11.

beats.cap: Here is the trick: training uses the exact same machine, but we already know the answer.
The target is just the sentence shifted by one word, so every position must guess its neighbour.
If the model is unsure about the right word, the loss is high. Backpropagation nudges the weights.
Every position is graded at once, so one sentence gives many little lessons.

lessons.title: Sequence Models: RNN & Seq2Seq
lessons.goal: Understand how recurrent networks turn a token sequence into context-aware hidden states, how an encoder-decoder maps one sequence to another, and why a single fixed context vector becomes a bottleneck.

cards.title: Same Word, Different Meaning
cards.text: An embedding table hands every token the same starting vector no matter where it appears. So 'bank' after a talk about interest rates and 'bank' after a walk by the river begin as identical points in space. That is a fine starting point, but real understanding needs contextual representations: vectors that shift depending on the neighbouring tokens because they absorb information from other positions. The big question for this whole chapter is therefore simple to state: how can a network move information between token positions so each vector learns what its context is?
points: Embedding lookup is context-independent: same ID, same vector
The initial embedding is only a learned token-level starting point
Contextual representations change with surrounding tokens
They are built by pulling in information from other positions
cards.example: 'After discussing interest rates, they went to the bank.' vs 'After walking along the river, they reached the bank.' - both 'bank' tokens start with the same embedding, but should end up meaning money vs riverside.
cards.say: An embedding gives the word bank the same vector whether we talk about money or a river. To really understand text, each word's vector must change with its context. The rest of this chapter is about how networks pass information between positions.
covers: B2: From static embeddings to contextual representations

items.tip: Embedding lookup: the same token ID always gives this exact same starting vector.
Words like interest, rates and loan live over here.
Words like shore, water and walk live over here.
After discussing interest rates, they went to the bank. Context pulls it toward money.
After walking along the river, they reached the bank. Context pulls it toward the shore.

beats.cap: Think of the word bank. Do you mean a place for money, or the grassy edge of a river?
An embedding table gives bank the exact same starting vector every time, no matter what sentence it sits in.
But after talk about interest rates it should mean money, and after a river walk it should mean shore.
So vectors must pull in information from neighbouring words. How to move that information is this chapter's big question.

cards.title: Two Ways to Move Information
cards.text: To build context, two jobs must be solved: propagation (getting information from earlier positions to later ones) and selection (finding which pieces matter). Recurrent neural networks, the classic sequence models, solve propagation by reading tokens strictly in order and updating a hidden state after every token. That hidden state acts like a running memory of everything seen so far. Attention, which comes later, instead opens weighted direct connections to any position. In both cases the architecture only fixes which information paths exist; training decides how much flows along each.
points: Propagation: earlier positions must reach later ones
Selection: the model must pick relevant information
RNNs read tokens in order and update a hidden state each step
The hidden state is the network's memory of the past
Attention: selective access through weighted connections
Architecture defines paths; training learns the parameters
cards.say: There are two classic ways to share information between words. A recurrent network passes a memory vector along the chain, one token at a time. Attention instead builds weighted shortcuts directly to any position. Training decides how information flows.

items.tip: An RNN processes token 1, then token 2, then token 3, strictly one after another.
After every token the hidden state is updated. It is a running summary of the past.
Propagation: early words reach later ones only by passing through every state in between.
Attention opens weighted connections straight to any position.
Selection: the model decides how much each position should contribute.
The architecture only fixes which paths exist. Training learns how much flows along each.

beats.cap: To build context, a model has two jobs. Carry information forward, and pick out the pieces that matter.
A recurrent network reads like you do, one word at a time, keeping a running memory called the hidden state.
Attention works differently, like flipping straight back to any page, with weights saying how much each one matters.
Either way, the design only builds the roads, and training decides how much traffic flows on each.

cards.title: Inside an RNN Step
cards.text: Take 'I love machine learning', four tokens processed at steps t = 1 to 4. At each step the token ID x_t selects one row of the embedding matrix, giving the vector e_t. The hidden layer then mixes two ingredients: the new embedding, through input-to-hidden weights, and the previous hidden state, through recurrent hidden-to-hidden weights. A bias is added and a nonlinearity such as tanh squashes the result into the new hidden state h_t. The very first state h_0 is all zeros. LSTMs replace this simple update with a gated, more elaborate one.
points: Pipeline per step: token ID -> embedding -> hidden -> linear -> softmax -> argmax
Embedding lookup: e_t = E[x_t], E has V rows of size d_e
W_he (H x d_e) maps the input, W_hh (H x H) carries the past
h_0 is a zero vector; H is the hidden size
LSTMs use a gated version of this update
cards.formula: e_t = E[x_t];  h_t = f(W_he e_t + W_hh h_(t-1) + b_h). x_t = token ID at step t, E = embedding matrix (V x d_e), W_he = input-to-hidden weights, W_hh = recurrent weights, b_h = bias, f = nonlinearity such as tanh, h_t = hidden state of size H.
cards.example: 'I love machine learning' -> 4 tokens -> 4 time steps; h_1 summarizes 'I', h_4 summarizes the whole sentence.
cards.say: At each step the RNN looks up the current word's embedding, mixes it with the previous hidden state using two weight matrices, adds a bias and applies a nonlinearity. The result is the new memory, passed on to the next word.
covers: A3: RNN forward pass: input and embedding layer

items.tip: Steps t = 1 to 4 for I, love, machine, learning. Each step brings one token ID.
The ID picks one row of the embedding matrix E, which has V rows of size d_e.
h_t = tanh of input weights times e_t plus recurrent weights times h_t-1 plus a bias.
The previous state feeds back in. h_0 starts as all zeros. LSTMs use a gated version.

beats.cap: Let's peek inside a recurrent network as it reads the sentence I love machine learning, one word per step.
Each word's ID picks one row from the embedding table, turning the word into a list of numbers.
The hidden layer mixes that new vector with its own memory from the previous step, then squashes the result.
Memory starts empty, so after four steps the final hidden state summarizes the whole sentence.

cards.title: From Hidden State to a Word
cards.text: A hidden state is not yet a prediction. A linear output layer projects h_t into a logit vector z_t holding one raw score for every vocabulary entry. Softmax then exponentiates each score and divides by the total, turning the logits into probabilities between 0 and 1 that add up to exactly one. The simplest choice of next token is argmax: take the most probable entry, which is called greedy search. Smarter selection rules based on sampling exist and are explained in the decoding lesson.
points: Output layer: W_0 is V x H, bias b_0 has V entries
Logits z_t: one unnormalized score per vocabulary token
Softmax turns logits into a probability distribution
Argmax picks the most likely token (greedy search)
Sampling-based alternatives come later
cards.formula: z_t = W_0 h_t + b_0;  p(y_t = i) = exp(z_t,i) / sum over j of exp(z_t,j);  y_t = argmax_i p(y_t = i). V = vocabulary size, H = hidden size.
cards.say: To turn memory into a word, a linear layer produces one score per vocabulary token. Softmax converts those scores into probabilities that add up to one, and the simplest strategy just picks the highest one. That is called greedy search.
covers: A3: Output projection, softmax and argmax

items.tip: Highest logit after I love machine: the greedy pick.
A sensible alternative with a lower score.
Possible, but less likely.
A very low score: almost zero chance after softmax.

beats.cap: A hidden state is just a bundle of numbers. How do we turn it into an actual next word?
A linear output layer gives every word in the vocabulary one raw score, called a logit.
Softmax turns those scores into chances between zero and one that add up to exactly one.
The simplest rule just takes the most likely word. That is greedy search. Try dragging the temperature too.

cards.title: Encoder Meets Decoder
cards.text: Translation, summarization, captioning and dialogue all turn one sequence into another, often of a different length. One RNN struggles to understand and generate at once, so seq2seq splits the work. An encoder RNN reads the whole input; its final hidden state becomes a fixed-size context vector, and its per-step outputs are thrown away. A decoder RNN starts from that vector as its initial state and generates tokens one by one, beginning with <bos> and feeding its own previous predictions back in. Both networks are trained jointly to maximise the probability of the correct output.
points: Tasks: translation, summarization, image captioning, dialogue
Encoder compresses the input into one context vector c
c = final encoder state = initial decoder state s_0
Decoder input: <bos> plus previously predicted tokens
Encoder and decoder are trained jointly; lengths may differ
Distant information must hop through every intermediate state
cards.formula: c = h_n (final encoder state) = s_0;  p(y_1..y_m | x_1..x_n) = product over t of p(y_t | y_<t, c). x = input tokens (n), y = output tokens (m).
cards.say: Sequence to sequence models use two recurrent networks. The encoder reads the input and squeezes it into one context vector. The decoder starts from that vector and writes the output word by word, feeding each prediction back in.

items.tip: Translation, summaries, image captions, dialogue: one sequence in, another out.
Reads the whole input. Its per-step outputs are thrown away.
The final encoder state. It also becomes the decoder's first state s_0.
Starts with <bos> and feeds its own earlier predictions back in.
Can have a different length. Both networks are trained together.

beats.cap: Translating is two jobs at once, understanding a sentence and then writing a new one, so why not use two networks?
The encoder reads the whole input and squeezes it into one fixed-size summary, the context vector.
The decoder starts from that summary and writes word by word, feeding each guess back in as its next input.
Both halves learn together, and the output can be shorter or longer than the input.

cards.title: Translating Step by Step
cards.text: Unroll the networks in time. The encoder reads 'I', 'love', 'machine', 'learning' and hands its last state to the decoder. The decoder receives <bos> and outputs 'Jag'; that word becomes its next input and produces 'älskar'; then 'maskininlärning' follows, and finally <eos> stops generation. Four English tokens became three Swedish ones, because 'machine learning' is a single compound word in Swedish. This shows nicely that encoder and decoder lengths are independent. For simplicity the time counter is restarted when the decoder begins.
points: Encoder unrolled over 4 input tokens
Decoder begins with <bos>
Each output is fed back as the next input
Generation ends when <eos> is produced
4 input tokens -> 3 output tokens plus <eos>
cards.example: 'I love machine learning' -> <bos> -> 'Jag' -> 'älskar' -> 'maskininlärning' -> <eos>.
cards.say: Here the encoder reads I love machine learning. The decoder starts with a begin token and writes Jag, then älskar, then maskininlärning, and finally an end token. Four English words became three Swedish ones.

items.tip: The encoder reads these 4 tokens and hands its final state to the decoder.
The begin token kicks off the decoder.
First Swedish word. It becomes the next decoder input.
Swedish for love.
One Swedish compound word for machine learning.
The end token stops generation.

beats.cap: Let's watch the machine translate I love machine learning into Swedish, one step at a time.
The decoder gets a start token and says Jag, then feeds Jag back in and says älskar.
Next comes maskininlärning, and finally an end token tells the decoder to stop.
Four English tokens became three Swedish words, because machine learning is a single compound word in Swedish.

cards.title: The Bottleneck Problem
cards.text: Basic seq2seq forces the entire source sentence through one fixed-size vector, and the decoder has no way to peek at individual encoder states. For short sentences this works surprisingly well. For long or complicated inputs, however, crucial details get crushed or forgotten, and translation or summary quality drops. A fixed-size container simply cannot scale with variable-length input. The cure, proposed by Bahdanau and colleagues, is attention: let the decoder look back at all encoder hidden states and assemble a new, tailored context vector at every decoding step.
points: Whole input squeezed into one context vector
Decoder cannot access individual encoder states
Fine for short sentences, lossy for long ones
Fixed size vs. variable-length input
Fix: attention builds a new context vector per step
cards.say: The weakness of basic seq2seq is that the whole sentence must fit into one fixed vector. Long sentences lose details. Attention fixes this by letting the decoder look back at every encoder state whenever it needs to.
covers: A3: Information bottleneck and motivation for attention

items.tip: Who is acting in the sentence.
What happens.
Who or what it happens to.
Past, present, future.
Exact details that are easy to lose.
Extra parts of a long sentence.
What survives the squeeze for a long input.

beats.cap: Imagine packing for a long trip into one small suitcase. Something important will be left behind.
Basic sequence to sequence squeezes the whole sentence into one fixed-size vector, and the decoder can never peek back.
For short sentences that works well, but long inputs lose crucial details and the translation gets worse.
The fix is attention, which lets the decoder look back at every encoder state and build a fresh summary each step.

lessons.title: Attention in Seq2Seq
lessons.goal: Learn how attention scores, softmax weights and a per-step context vector let an RNN decoder look back at every source word, and why this beat the fixed-context seq2seq model.

cards.title: Scoring Every Source Word
cards.text: Back to 'I love machine learning', now with attention. Before the decoder writes its first word, the encoder has already produced four hidden states h_1 to h_4, one per source token, and the decoder state starts as s_0 = h_4 = c. For every encoder position the model computes a score: how well does the current decoder state match this source state, i.e. how relevant is that word right now? Luong attention simply takes a dot product. Bahdanau attention learns an additive score with a tiny feed-forward network. Either way, one number per source word comes out.
points: Encoder states h_1..h_4 exist before decoding (h_0 = 0)
Initial decoder state s_0 = h_4 = c
Score a_t,i rates the match of s_(t-1) with h_i
Luong: dot-product score
Bahdanau: learned additive score
Answers: how much should step t attend to position i?
cards.formula: a_t,i = score(s_(t-1), h_i). Luong dot product: score(s, h) = s . h. Bahdanau additive: score(s, h) = v^T tanh(W_s s + W_h h). s = decoder state, h_i = encoder state at position i, v, W_s, W_h = learned parameters.
cards.example: Step t = 1: decoder input <bos>, four scores a_1,1 .. a_1,4, one for each of 'I', 'love', 'machine', 'learning'.
cards.say: With attention, the decoder first compares its current state with every encoder state. Each comparison gives a relevance score. Luong attention uses a plain dot product, while Bahdanau attention learns a small scoring network.
covers: A4: Attention scores, distribution and context vector

items.tip: Score a_1,1: how well the decoder state s_0 matches encoder state h_1. Values are illustrative.
Score a_1,2 compares s_0 with h_2.
Score a_1,3 compares s_0 with h_3.
Score a_1,4. Note s_0 = h_4 = c, the old context vector, is where the decoder starts.

beats.cap: Before writing a word, the decoder asks a simple question. Which source words matter to me right now?
The encoder has already left one state behind for each word, I, love, machine and learning.
The decoder compares its current state with each one and gets a relevance score per word.
Luong attention scores with a plain dot product, while Bahdanau attention learns a tiny scoring network.

cards.title: Weights and the Context Vector
cards.text: Raw scores can be any size, so softmax converts them into an attention distribution: positive weights that sum to one. The context vector for this step is then the weighted sum of all encoder states, a summary of the source tuned to what the decoder needs at this exact moment. At the very first step the slides show a uniform 0.25 for each of the four words; that picture is only illustrative, since real weights already depend on the states. The key change from plain seq2seq: a brand new context vector is computed at every decoding step.
points: Softmax over scores gives weights alpha_t,i
Weights are positive and sum to 1
Context c_t = weighted sum of encoder states
Uniform 0.25 weights at t = 1 are illustrative only
A fresh context vector at every step
cards.formula: alpha_t,i = exp(a_t,i) / sum over j of exp(a_t,j);  c_t = sum over i of alpha_t,i h_i. alpha = attention weights, c_t = context vector at step t.
cards.example: t = 1 with 4 encoder states: alpha_1,i is about 0.25 each, so c_1 = 0.25 (h_1 + h_2 + h_3 + h_4) in the illustrative uniform case.
cards.say: Softmax turns the scores into weights that are positive and add up to one. The context vector is the weighted average of the encoder states, so every decoding step gets its own custom summary of the source sentence.
covers: B2: Attention distribution and context vector
A4: Attention scores, distribution and context vector

items.tip: Scores can be any size, even negative.
alpha = exp of each score divided by the sum of all exps.
At t = 1 the picture shows 0.25 each. That uniform split is only illustrative.
c_1 = 0.25 times h_1 + h_2 + h_3 + h_4 in the illustrative uniform case.
A custom summary of the source, rebuilt at every decoding step.

beats.cap: Raw scores are messy numbers, so softmax turns them into tidy weights that are positive and add up to one.
In the simple picture each of the four words gets a quarter, though real weights depend on the states.
Then we blend the encoder states using those weights, like mixing paint with a recipe of proportions.
The big change from plain sequence to sequence is that a brand new context vector is made at every single step.

cards.title: Updating the Decoder
cards.text: Now the decoder computes its new state from three ingredients: the embedding of the token it produced last, its own previous state, and the fresh context vector. Bahdanau and colleagues used gated recurrent units, GRUs, for this update. The new state then goes through an output layer to get logits over the target vocabulary, softmax turns them into probabilities, and a selection rule such as argmax picks the word. In the example, step one starts from <bos>, uses context c_1, produces state s_1 and outputs 'Jag'.
points: New state uses previous token embedding, s_(t-1) and c_t
Bahdanau et al. used GRU cells
Output layer -> softmax -> argmax gives the token
The chosen token is fed back as the next input
First output in the example: 'Jag'
cards.formula: s_t = f_dec(e_(t-1), s_(t-1), c_t);  p(y_t | y_<t, x) = softmax(W_o s_t + b_o);  y_t = argmax p. f_dec = recurrent cell such as a GRU, e_(t-1) = embedding of previous output.
cards.example: t = 1: input <bos> + context c_1 -> state s_1 -> output 'Jag'.
cards.say: The decoder now updates its memory using the last word it wrote, its previous state and the new context vector. In the original work this was a GRU cell. Then an output layer and softmax choose the next word, here Jag.
covers: B2: Decoder update and output with attention
A4: Decoder update and step-by-step translation

items.tip: Ingredients: embedding of the previous output and the previous state s_t-1. At t = 1 that is <bos>.
The fresh attention summary for this step.
Computed by a recurrent cell. Bahdanau and colleagues used GRUs.
Logits over the target vocabulary become probabilities.
Argmax picks the most likely word. It is fed back as the next input.

beats.cap: Now the decoder cooks its new memory from three ingredients, like a chef combining leftovers with a fresh delivery.
The last word, the old state and the fresh context vector go into a recurrent cell, which was a GRU originally.
The new state goes through an output layer and softmax, and the most likely word is picked.
At step one that word is Jag, and it is fed straight back in to start the next round.

cards.title: Watching Attention Move
cards.text: The whole cycle of scores, weights, context and state update repeats at every step, so attention can wander across the source. When writing the second word, the weight on 'love' clearly dominates and the decoder emits 'älskar'. At the next step attention shifts onto 'machine' and 'learning', which together become the single Swedish compound 'maskininlärning'. Finally <eos> ends the output. Each target word thus draws on exactly the source words it corresponds to. The weights drawn in the figures are illustrative, but the mechanism is the real one.
points: Scores, weights and context recomputed every step
t = 2: focus on 'love' -> 'älskar'
t = 3: focus on 'machine' + 'learning' -> 'maskininlärning'
Last step emits <eos>
Figure weights are illustrative
cards.formula: For each step t: a_t,i = score(s_(t-1), h_i); alpha_t = softmax(a_t); c_t = sum over i of alpha_t,i h_i; s_t = f_dec(e_(t-1), s_(t-1), c_t).
cards.example: <bos> -> 'Jag' -> 'älskar' -> 'maskininlärning' -> <eos>. At t = 2 the weight alpha_2,2 on 'love' is by far the largest.
cards.say: Watch the attention move. For the second word the decoder focuses on love and writes älskar. Then it looks at machine and learning and writes maskininlärning. Finally it produces the end token.
covers: A4: Decoder update and step-by-step translation

items.tip: Source word 1.
Source word 2.
Source word 3.
Source word 4.
t = 1: written right after <bos>.
t = 2: the weight on love is by far the largest.
t = 3: attention spreads over machine and learning. Then <eos> ends the output.

beats.cap: Like a spotlight on a stage, attention moves to a new spot every time the decoder writes a word.
For the second word, the spotlight lands almost fully on love, and the decoder writes älskar.
Then it shines on machine and learning together, which become the single word maskininlärning, and an end token follows.
Every target word draws on exactly the source words it matches. The drawn weights are illustrative, the mechanism is real.

cards.title: Reading an Attention Map
cards.text: Collect all weights into a grid and you get an attention map: one row per generated target word, one column per source word, brighter cells for stronger attention. Because the decoder reads a different sequence than its own, this is cross-attention. In translation maps the bright cells often run along a diagonal, since words tend to align in order. Where the two languages order words differently, the bright path bends, showing that attention learned the reordering. Nobody labelled these alignments; they emerge from the input and the trained parameters.
points: Rows = target tokens, columns = source tokens
Cell brightness = attention weight
Often near-diagonal alignment
Bends capture word reordering (non-monotonic alignment)
Patterns are computed dynamically, not hand-coded
cards.formula: A[t, i] = alpha_t,i (row t = output position, column i = input position).
cards.example: Figure 3(a) of Bahdanau et al. 2014: an English-French attention map with a mostly diagonal bright path that bends where word order differs.
cards.say: An attention map shows all weights as a heat grid. Target words are rows, source words are columns. In translation the bright cells often follow a diagonal, and they bend wherever the languages put words in a different order.

items.tip: Row 1: bright on I.
Row 2: bright on love.
Row 3: bright on machine and learning.
Last row: the end of the output.

beats.cap: Collect every weight into one picture, like a heat map, and you can see where the model looked.
Each row is a word the decoder wrote, each column a source word, and brighter cells mean stronger attention.
Because the decoder reads another sequence, this is cross-attention, and the bright cells often run down a diagonal.
Where languages order words differently, the path bends. Nobody labelled this, the model learned the alignment itself.

cards.title: What Attention Bought Us
cards.text: Attention delivered large accuracy gains in neural machine translation. It removes the bottleneck, because every output step builds its own content-dependent summary instead of relying on one memory vector, a bit like a human translator re-reading the relevant part of the sentence. It creates short, direct paths between distant positions, which also shortens gradient paths and eases vanishing gradients. And its weights act as a soft alignment learned without any alignment labels. Two caveats: attention maps help inspection but are not full explanations, and at this stage encoder and decoder are still recurrent.
points: Large accuracy gains over fixed-context seq2seq
Dynamic per-step context removes the bottleneck
Direct paths shorten information and gradient routes
Soft alignment learned without supervision
Maps aid inspection but do not fully explain predictions
Encoder and decoder are still RNNs
cards.say: Attention made translation much better. It removes the bottleneck, gives gradients short direct paths, and its weights reveal learned word alignments. But the encoder and decoder were still recurrent, which the Transformer will change next.
covers: A4: Advantages of the attention mechanism
B2: What attention adds to RNN seq2seq

items.tip: Gave large accuracy gains in neural machine translation.
Each output step builds its own summary instead of one memory vector.
Direct links between distant words also shorten gradient paths and ease vanishing gradients.
The weights act as a soft word alignment, learned without alignment labels.
Attention maps help inspection but are not full explanations of a prediction.
Encoder and decoder are still recurrent. The Transformer changes that next.

beats.cap: So what did attention buy us? Translations got much better, almost overnight.
Like a human translator re-reading the right part of a sentence, every step gets its own summary, so the bottleneck is gone.
Direct links connect distant words, which also helps learning, and the weights reveal word alignments for free.
Two caveats. Maps are not full explanations, and the encoder and decoder are still recurrent networks.

lessons.title: Self-Attention: Queries, Keys, Values
lessons.goal: Understand how the Transformer replaces recurrence with self-attention, how queries, keys and values are projected and combined by scaled dot-product attention, and why several heads run in parallel.

cards.title: Attention Is All You Need
cards.text: In 2017 a NeurIPS paper by Vaswani and colleagues asked a bold question: what if we drop recurrence entirely and keep only attention? The resulting Transformer was built for machine translation with two stacks of N layers. The encoder reads the input with bidirectional self-attention; the decoder writes the output with causal self-attention that cannot see future tokens, and cross-attention lets decoder queries read the encoder outputs. With no recurrent chain, all known positions are processed in parallel, so training scales on modern hardware. Generation, however, still happens one token at a time.
points: NeurIPS 2017; about 200,000 citations by Sep 2025 and about 300,000 by Nov 2026
Ranked 7th most cited paper of the 21st century by Nature
Encoder: bidirectional self-attention; decoder: causal self-attention
Cross-attention links decoder queries to encoder outputs
Parallel over known positions; generation stays sequential
Basis of BERT, GPT and other foundation models
cards.example: Layer ingredients: positional encoding added to embeddings, (masked) multi-head attention, feed-forward network, residual connections and layer normalization; already familiar parts are token IDs, shifted-right outputs, embeddings, final linear layer, softmax and greedy selection.
cards.say: In twenty seventeen, the paper Attention Is All You Need removed recurrence completely. The Transformer uses only attention, so all positions can be processed in parallel during training. It became the foundation of BERT, GPT and nearly every modern language model.
covers: A4: Attention Is All You Need and the Transformer overview
B3: Attention Is All You Need and the original encoder-decoder Transformer

items.tip: Encoder and decoder RNNs read and write strictly one token at a time.
The decoder learns to look back at every encoder state, but the networks stay recurrent.
Attention Is All You Need, NeurIPS 2017: encoder and decoder stacks of N layers, no recurrence.
Foundation models built on Transformer parts. Nature ranked the paper 7th most cited of the century.
About 200,000 citations by September 2025, and still climbing fast.

beats.cap: What if we threw away the recurrent chain completely and kept only attention? In twenty seventeen one famous paper tried exactly that.
The Transformer has an encoder that sees the whole input, and a decoder that cannot peek at future words.
Cross-attention lets the decoder read the encoder, and with no chain, all known positions train in parallel on modern hardware.
Writing still happens one token at a time, yet this design became the basis of BERT, GPT and nearly every modern model.

cards.title: From Cross- to Self-Attention
cards.text: In the RNN translator, attention let the decoder read from a different sequence, the encoder's states; that is cross-attention. Self-attention turns the same trick inward: every position in a sequence gathers information from the other positions of that very sequence. It works in three moves: decide how relevant each other position is, convert relevance into weights, and aggregate the information. Because no hidden state is handed along a chain, all positions can be updated at the same time, and the result is a context-dependent vector for every token.
points: Recurrence: information flows through successive states
Attention: weighted direct access, computed for the current position
Cross-attention reads another sequence; self-attention reads its own
Three steps: relevance, weights, aggregation
No recurrent chain, so positions update in parallel
cards.formula: updated_i = sum over j of w_ij * info_j. w_ij = relevance weight of position j for position i.
cards.example: 'After walking along the river, they reached the bank.' - the updated vector for 'bank' draws heavily on 'river', pointing to a riverbank (illustrative weights).
cards.say: Cross-attention looks into another sequence. Self-attention looks inside the same sentence. Every word decides which other words matter, weights them, and mixes in their information. In the river example, bank borrows meaning from river.

items.tip: Weight about 0.05 from bank.
Weight about 0.08 from bank.
Bank draws most heavily here, which points to a riverbank. Weights are illustrative.
Weight about 0.05 from bank.
Weight about 0.07 from bank.
Its updated vector is a weighted sum of information from the whole sentence.

beats.cap: Earlier, the decoder looked into a different sentence, the encoder's. That is called cross-attention.
Self-attention turns the trick inward, so every word looks at the other words of its very own sentence.
Each word decides who is relevant, turns that into weights, and mixes in their information. Bank borrows heavily from river.
No memory is passed down a chain, so all words can update at the same time into context-aware vectors.

cards.title: Query, Key, Value
cards.text: Attention becomes clearer if we split it into three roles. Think of a library. Your search request, say 'books about quantum computing', is the query. Each book's index card with keywords like 'physics', 'quantum', 'algorithms' is a key. The book's actual contents are the value. You compare the query with every key, normalize the matches with softmax, and read a weighted blend of the values. Bahdanau attention already fits this pattern: the decoder state supplies the query, encoder states supply keys and values. When queries come from the decoder and keys and values from the encoder, we call it cross-attention.
points: Query: what am I looking for?
Key: what can I be matched on?
Value: what information do I hand over?
Dot-product scores, softmax, weighted sum of values
Output = context vector passed onward
Decoder queries on encoder keys/values = cross-attention
cards.formula: q_t = s_(t-1) W_Q;  k_i = h_i W_K;  v_i = h_i W_V;  e_t,i = q_t . k_i;  alpha_t,i = softmax_i(e_t,i);  c_t = sum over i of alpha_t,i v_i.
cards.example: Library: query 'Find books related to quantum computing'; keys = index-card keywords 'physics', 'quantum', 'algorithms', 'computing'; values = the books themselves.
cards.say: Think of a library. Your search request is the query, each index card is a key, and the book content is the value. Compare the query with all keys, turn the matches into weights, and read a weighted mix of the values.
covers: A4: Query, key, value: generalizing attention
B3: Queries, keys, values and their learned projections

items.tip: Key: quantum, computing. Strong match, so its value, the book's content, gets a big weight.
Key: quantum, algorithms. Good match.
Key: physics. A partial match, small weight.
Key: cooking. Almost no match, nearly zero weight.
Key: gardening. No match.

beats.cap: Picture a library. You walk in with a request, find books about quantum computing. That request is the query.
Every book has an index card of keywords, the key, and the book's actual content is the value.
You compare your query with every key, softmax turns the matches into weights, and you read a blend of the best values.
When the queries come from the decoder and the keys and values from the encoder, we call it cross-attention.

cards.title: Learned Q, K, V Projections
cards.text: Where do queries, keys and values come from in self-attention? Each token's input vector x_i (embedding plus position, or the previous layer's output) is multiplied by three separate learned matrices. W_Q and W_K map into a shared comparison space, while W_V maps into a space tuned for carrying information. The matrices are shared by all positions inside one layer but differ between layers. Queries and keys must have the same size d_k so their dot product exists; values may use a different size d_v. In the original Transformer, d_model = 512 and d_k = d_v = 64 per head.
points: Three separate linear projections per layer
Shared across positions, different in every layer
W_Q, W_K: comparison space; W_V: information space
d_q = d_k required for the dot product; d_v may differ
Original model: d_model = 512, d_k = d_v = 64
Architecture fixes the shapes; training learns the values
cards.formula: q_i = x_i W_Q, k_i = x_i W_K, v_i = x_i W_V. x_i = row vector of size d_model; W_Q, W_K have shape d_model x d_k; W_V has shape d_model x d_v.
cards.example: Query of 'bank' vs keys of After, walking, river, reached, bank -> weights .08, .07, .65, .08, .12; the largest, .65, lands on 'river'.
cards.say: Each token vector is multiplied by three learned matrices to get its query, key and value. Queries and keys must have the same length so they can be compared. In the original model, the model width is five hundred twelve and each head uses sixty four.
covers: B3: Queries, keys, values and their learned projections
A4: Query, key, value: generalizing attention
