cards.example: Illustrative mix: web 70% of available data -> 40% of training (down), books 15% -> 20% (up), code 10% -> 25% (up), math 5% -> 15% (up). Math at 15% of tokens from 5% of data means each math document is seen about three times.
cards.say: A data mixture decides how many training tokens come from each source. Small valuable sources such as code or math get boosted, while the huge pile of web text gets turned down.

items.tip: General web pages dominate what is available.
Downsampled: the model reads less web than exists.
Valuable long-form prose.
Upsampled a little.
Small but useful.
Upsampled strongly.
Scarce, high value.
15% of tokens from 5% of data: each math document is seen about three times.

beats.cap: Like cooking, having a whole sack of flour does not mean the cake should be mostly flour.
Web text is seventy percent of what we have, but it gets only forty percent of training.
Small, precious sources like books, code and math are upsampled, read more often and even repeated.
The token budget is fixed, so every extra percent for math is taken from another source.

cards.title: Synthetic Textbooks: Phi-1
cards.text: Sometimes the best data has to be written on purpose. Microsoft's Phi-1 (2023) is a 1.3B-parameter model for Python code. Its creators picked useful existing code, defined topics and target audiences, and asked GPT-3.5 to generate textbook-style explanations with annotated examples. The model was pretrained on this blend of filtered real and synthetic material, then finetuned on generated exercises with solutions. In a controlled 350M-parameter test, adding the synthetic textbooks raised the share of solutions passing unit tests from 17.7% to 20.1%, without more parameters. The takeaway: data is an engineering design choice, though synthetic data is not automatically superior.
points: Phi-1: Microsoft 2023, 1.3B parameters, Python code
GPT-3.5 writes textbook-style lessons and examples
Pretrain on real + synthetic, finetune on generated exercises
350M test: pass rate 17.7% -> 20.1% (+2.4 pp)
Does not prove synthetic data always wins
cards.example: A synthetic lesson on filtering even numbers: keep n when n % 2 == 0, so [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6] becomes [2, 4, 6]. Pass rate (350M model): filtered web plus code 17.7%, plus synthetic textbooks 20.1%.
cards.say: Phi one was trained partly on textbooks written by another language model. In a small controlled test, those synthetic lessons raised the share of correct code solutions from about eighteen to twenty percent.

items.tip: Phi-1, Microsoft 2023: a 1.3B-parameter model for Python.
Topics and target audiences are defined up front.
Textbook-style lessons, like keeping even numbers so 1..6 becomes 2, 4, 6.
Filtered real code plus synthetic textbooks.
Generated exercises with solutions.
350M test model: solutions passing unit tests rose 2.4 points. Synthetic is not automatically better.

beats.cap: Sometimes the perfect textbook does not exist yet, so you simply ask an AI to write it.
For the small coding model Phi one, its makers picked good code and chose topics to teach.
A bigger model wrote friendly lessons with examples, then Phi one studied them and practiced exercises.
In a small test, working solutions rose from about eighteen to twenty percent, with no extra size.

cards.title: Bias Lives in the Data
cards.text: A language model is rewarded for predicting text well, not for being right or fair. It therefore copies whatever correlations its corpus contains, including unfair ones. Web text mirrors human behavior and media production, and some groups, regions and viewpoints are far louder online than others, so predictions tend to favor the overrepresented. Worse, training can amplify small asymmetries: if men appear only slightly more often than women in leadership contexts, the model may form a strong, systematic association. Bias is thus best understood as a property of the data distribution, which itself reflects value-laden human choices.
points: Objective rewards likely text, not true or fair text
Models replicate correlations, including harmful ones
Web corpora overrepresent some voices
Training can amplify small skews into systematic patterns
Bias is a property of the data distribution
cards.example: Slight data skew: men mentioned a bit more often than women in leadership sentences -> the model links leadership with men much more strongly in its outputs.
cards.say: Models learn correlations, not truth. If the data slightly favors one group, the trained model can turn that small tilt into a strong and systematic bias.

items.tip: Equal mentions in the data: no learned preference.
Men mentioned a bit more often than women in leadership sentences.
The model can link leadership with men much more strongly than the data did.

beats.cap: A model is rewarded for guessing likely text, not true or fair text. It copies what it reads.
The web is not balanced: some groups, regions and opinions are much louder than others.
Say men appear just a bit more often than women in sentences about leaders.
Training can blow that small tilt up into a strong habit, so bias really lives in the data.

cards.title: The Language Gap
cards.text: Language bias is easy to measure. For the GPT-4 report, the MMLU benchmark of multiple-choice questions across many subjects was translated into numerous languages and the same model was tested on each. English scored highest at 85.5%, while Telugu reached only 62.0%, and low-resource languages generally lagged. A likely main cause is that English dominates the training data. Other contributors may be less efficient tokenization, which spends more tokens per sentence on some scripts, translation quality of the test, and some languages simply being harder to model. Careful: the scores show the gap but do not by themselves prove which cause matters most.
points: MMLU translated into many languages, same model (GPT-4)
English 85.5% vs Telugu 62.0%
Low-resource languages score lower
Likely causes: data imbalance, tokenization, translation effects
A measured gap does not prove its cause
cards.example: GPT-4 on translated MMLU: English 85.5% (best) vs Telugu 62.0%, a gap of 23.5 percentage points, compared with English making up about 46% of Common Crawl.
cards.say: When GPT four took the same exam in different languages, it scored eighty five and a half percent in English but only sixty two percent in Telugu, largely because English dominates its training data.

items.tip: Best score of all languages. English is about 46% of Common Crawl.
23.5 points lower. Low-resource languages generally lag behind.

beats.cap: Here is an easy experiment: give the same model the same quiz, translated into many languages.
In English the model scored eighty five and a half percent, its best result.
In Telugu it reached only sixty two percent, and other less common languages also lagged.
English dominating the data is the likely main cause, but tokenization and translation may play a part too.

lessons.title: Pretraining: Objective & Compute
lessons.goal: Understand the self-supervised next-token objective and its cross-entropy loss, how the learning rate and batches are scheduled, and how FLOPs and GPU hardware set the cost of pretraining.

cards.title: The Pretraining Objective
cards.text: Pretraining teaches an LLM with one simple self-supervised task: given all previous tokens, predict the next one. Raw text supplies its own labels, because the target sequence is just the input shifted right by one position. In each forward pass the model turns every position into a probability distribution over the vocabulary, and causal masking stops a position from peeking at future tokens. That lets all positions of a sequence be trained at once. The result is a language model that has absorbed grammar, facts and style purely from predicting text.
points: Objective: maximize p(next token | all previous tokens)
Self-supervised: the raw text is its own label
Target = input sequence shifted right by one position
Causal masking blocks future tokens, so all positions train in parallel
cards.formula: p_theta(x_{t+1} | x_<=t) = probability of the next token given all previous tokens; theta = model parameters
cards.example: Input 'The cat sat on the', target 'mat'; the model scores every word in its vocabulary, and the true next word gets one probability.
cards.say: Pretraining uses a single task: guess the next word. The text itself provides the answers, because the target is just the input shifted by one. Causal masking keeps the model honest by hiding future words.
covers: B6: Next-token prediction and cross-entropy loss
A6: Next-token prediction and cross-entropy loss

scene.text: The cat sat on the mat

items.tip: Input position 1. Its target is the next token: cat.
Target for 'The'. Also an input whose target is 'sat'.
The target sequence is just the input shifted right by one position.
Causal masking: this position can only look back, never ahead.
Every position predicts its next token in the same forward pass.
Target for 'The cat sat on the'. The model scores every vocabulary word; 'mat' gets one probability.

beats.cap: Pretraining is one simple game, played trillions of times: read the words so far and guess the next one.
No teacher writes answers. The text grades itself, because each word's answer is simply the word after it.
A mask hides the future, so every word only sees words before it, and all positions practice at once.
Given the cat sat on the, the model scores every word it knows, hoping mat gets a high chance.

cards.title: Cross-Entropy Loss
cards.text: The training signal is cross-entropy loss: the negative log of the probability the model gave to the correct next token. A confident correct answer gives a small loss, while a low probability gives a large one. The loss is averaged over every position and billions of tokens, backpropagation computes its gradient with respect to all parameters, and an optimizer nudges the weights to raise the probability of what actually came next. Minimizing cross-entropy is exactly maximizing the likelihood of the training text.
points: Loss = -log p(correct next token)
Low target probability -> high loss
Averaged over all positions and billions of tokens
Backpropagation gives gradients; the optimizer updates weights
Minimizing cross-entropy = maximizing data likelihood
cards.formula: L(theta) = -(1/T) * sum_t log P_theta(x_t | x_<t); single position L = -log p(target)
cards.example: For 'The cat sat on the mat.' the model gives p('mat') = 0.10, so the loss is -ln(0.10) ≈ 2.30. Raising that probability to 0.9 drops the loss to about 0.11.
cards.say: Cross entropy just measures how much probability the model gave the right word. A low probability means a big loss, so training pushes that probability up until the loss for the right word is tiny.
covers: B6: Next-token prediction and cross-entropy loss
A6: Next-token prediction and cross-entropy loss

scene.xl: chance given to the right word

items.tip: Loss = minus the natural log of 0.10, about 2.30. A big penalty.
Minus ln 0.90 is about 0.11. Confident and correct: almost no penalty.

beats.cap: How do we tell the model how wrong it was? We look at the chance it gave the right word.
For the cat sat on the mat, it gave mat only a ten percent chance, so the loss is a big two point three.
Push that chance up to ninety percent and the loss shrinks to about one tenth.
Averaged over billions of words, backpropagation finds which way to nudge every weight to raise the right word's chance.

cards.title: Warm-Up and Cosine Decay
cards.text: Training is very sensitive to the learning rate, so it follows a schedule. It begins with a linear warm-up, rising from near zero to a peak, because early on the weights are random and Adam's running estimates of the gradient mean and variance are still unreliable; large steps there could destabilize training. After the peak a cosine curve decays the rate smoothly to a small minimum, giving finer updates near the end and avoiding loss spikes. Linear warm-up plus cosine decay is the standard recipe behind models such as GPT-3 and Llama 2/3.
points: Adam scales each step by the gradient mean over its root-mean-square
Warm-up: linear ramp from ~0 to the peak learning rate
Protects Adam's still-unreliable moment estimates early on
Cosine decay: smooth drop to a small final learning rate
Warm-up is usually 1k-10k steps; decay spans millions
Used in GPT-3 and Llama 2/3
cards.formula: Warm-up: eta(t) = eta_max * t / T_warmup; Cosine: eta(t) = eta_min + 0.5(eta_max - eta_min)(1 + cos(pi (t - T_warmup)/(T_total - T_warmup)))
cards.example: Peak learning rate is reached after a warm-up of about 1,000-10,000 steps, then decayed along a cosine curve to a small final value across millions of optimizer steps.
cards.say: Training starts with a gentle warm up, because Adam needs time to trust its own estimates. Then the learning rate glides down along a cosine curve, so the model settles smoothly instead of overshooting at the end.
covers: B6: Learning-rate schedules: warm-up and cosine decay
A6: Learning rate schedules: warm-up, cosine decay and Adam

items.tip: Weights are random and Adam's running mean and variance estimates are still unreliable.
Rate rises in a straight line, usually over 1,000 to 10,000 steps.
The largest step size, reached at the end of warm-up.
A smooth cosine-shaped glide down across millions of optimizer steps.
Fine updates at the end avoid loss spikes. Used for GPT-3 and Llama 2 and 3.

beats.cap: The learning rate is the size of each training step, and the model is very sensitive to it.
Like warming up before a run, we start tiny and ramp up, because the optimizer cannot trust its estimates yet.
After a few thousand steps at the peak, the rate glides down along a smooth cosine curve.
Tiny final steps let the model settle gently instead of overshooting. GPT three and Llama use this recipe.

cards.title: Batches and Optimizer Steps
cards.text: A batch is the set of examples whose gradients are combined into a single optimizer update. Each example is a token sequence of length L, so a batch of B sequences holds B times L tokens; only after the whole batch is processed does the loss, the gradients and one weight update happen. Small batches give noisy, unstable gradients, while large batches give smoother ones and better hardware use, though not automatically faster convergence. Modern LLM pretraining uses very large effective batches, often millions of tokens per step.
points: Batch = examples contributing to one optimizer update
Tokens per batch = B (sequences) x L (sequence length)
One batch: compute loss, compute gradients, then one update
Small batch: noisy, unstable gradients
Large batch: smoother gradients, better efficiency
LLM batches reach millions of tokens per step
cards.formula: T_batch = B * L  (tokens per batch; B = sequences per batch, L = sequence length)
cards.example: A batch of 2,048 sequences of length 4,096 tokens holds about 8.4 million tokens, all contributing to a single optimizer update.
cards.say: A batch is everything the optimizer sees before one update. Big batches give steadier gradients and are more efficient on hardware, and large models use batches of millions of tokens per step.

items.tip: Each row is one token sequence of length L = 4,096.
Every sequence adds its tokens to the same batch.
Small batches give noisy, unstable gradients.
Large batches give smoother gradients and better hardware use, but not automatically faster convergence.
B = 2,048 sequences. Tokens per batch = B x L ≈ 8.4 million.

beats.cap: Instead of learning from one sentence at a time, the model studies a whole stack of them together.
That stack is a batch: the model reads all of it, then makes just one weight update.
Tiny batches give jumpy, noisy directions, while big batches average out into a smoother path.
Two thousand forty eight sequences of four thousand ninety six tokens make about eight point four million tokens per step.

cards.title: FLOPs and the Cost of Training
cards.text: A FLOP is one floating-point operation, and a fused multiply-add counts as two. Transformers are dominated by huge matrix multiplications, so the FLOP count sets the compute, cost and time of a training run. A standard rule of thumb is about 6 FLOPs per parameter per token: two for the forward pass and four for the backward pass, ignoring attention overhead. Compute then grows linearly with parameters and tokens, while the attention part grows quadratically with sequence length. Training time is roughly total FLOPs divided by achieved FLOP/s.
points: FLOP = one floating-point operation; FMA = 2 FLOPs
FLOPs = total work; FLOP/s = hardware speed
~6 FLOPs per parameter per token (2 forward, 4 backward)
Compute scales linearly with parameters and tokens per step
Attention scales quadratically with sequence length
Depth is cheaper than width
cards.formula: C_train ~ 6 * N_params * T_batch  (FLOPs per optimizer step); Training time ~ total FLOPs / achieved FLOP/s
cards.example: With 2,048 tokens per step: a 7B model needs 6 * 7e9 * 2048 ≈ 8.6e13 FLOPs per step, while a 70B model needs ≈ 8.6e14 FLOPs, roughly ten times more.
cards.say: Every training step costs about six operations per parameter per token, two going forward and four coming back. That is trillions of operations per step, and the compute scales up with both the model and the batch.
covers: A6: FLOPs and the compute cost of training

items.tip: 6 x 7e9 parameters x 2,048 tokens ≈ 8.6e13 FLOPs per step.
Ten times the parameters, so ≈ 8.6e14 FLOPs: ten times more work.

beats.cap: A FLOP is one tiny math operation, like a single multiply. Training needs an astronomical number of them.
The rule of thumb is six per weight per token: two going forward and four coming back.
So a seven billion model with two thousand tokens per step needs about eighty six trillion operations each step.
Make the model ten times bigger and every step costs ten times more, since cost grows with size and tokens.

cards.title: Why GPUs: The H100
cards.text: CPUs have a few powerful general cores; GPUs have thousands of parallel units built for the matrix math that dominates training. They also add Tensor Cores for low-precision multiply-accumulate, very high memory bandwidth for moving weights and activations, and fast interconnects such as NVLink for multi-GPU work. Because training is often memory-bound, bandwidth matters as much as raw compute. The NVIDIA H100 shows the scale: 80 GB of HBM3, 3.35 TB/s of bandwidth, NVLink up to 900 GB/s, support from FP32 down to FP8, and up to 700 W.
points: CPU: few versatile cores; GPU: thousands of parallel units
Tensor Cores accelerate low-precision matrix math
Training is often memory-bound, so bandwidth matters
H100: 80 GB HBM3, 3.35 TB/s, NVLink 900 GB/s, up to 700 W
Memory limits model, batch and context size per GPU
An H100 cost around 35,000 EUR in late 2025
cards.example: A CPU reaches about 0.5-2 TFLOP/s and 50-100 GB/s of bandwidth, while a GPU offers thousands of TFLOP/s and multiple TB/s, turning training from years on CPUs into days or weeks on GPU clusters.
cards.say: Training runs on GPUs because they do thousands of matrix operations at once and move data incredibly fast. A single H100 packs eighty gigabytes of memory and more than three terabytes per second of bandwidth.
covers: B6: GPUs for LLM training (NVIDIA H100)
A6: Hardware: CPU vs. GPU and the NVIDIA H100

items.tip: Versatile, great for general tasks, not for giant matrix math.
Built for the parallel matrix math that dominates training, plus Tensor Cores for low precision.
Roughly the compute of a CPU.
Training goes from years on CPUs to days or weeks on GPU clusters.
CPU memory bandwidth.
H100: 80 GB HBM3. Training is often memory-bound, so bandwidth matters as much as compute.
Fast GPU-to-GPU links. Up to 700 W; around 35,000 EUR in late 2025.

beats.cap: A CPU is like a few brilliant chefs, while a GPU is like a thousand cooks chopping at once.
Training is mostly huge piles of matrix math, so the thousand cooks win by a mile.
Moving data matters as much as math, and one H100 holds eighty gigabytes and moves over three terabytes per second.
Fast links tie many GPUs together, turning years of training into days or weeks.

lessons.title: Numbers & Parallelism
lessons.goal: Understand how numeric precision, memory limits and the four families of parallelism (data, tensor, pipeline and 3D with ZeRO) let training scale beyond one GPU, and what a finished base model looks like.

cards.title: Numeric Precision Formats
cards.text: Every weight, activation, gradient and optimizer state is stored in a numeric format, and that choice affects stability, memory, speed, bandwidth and how big a model or batch fits. In floating point, exponent bits set the representable range and fraction bits set precision. FP16 is more accurate than BF16 near 1.0 but has a tiny range and needs loss scaling. BF16 keeps FP32's 8 exponent bits with only 7 fraction bits, so it is stable, half the size, and the standard for training. FP8 speeds up supported GPUs; INT8 and INT4 serve inference and QLoRA.
points: Format affects stability, memory, speed, bandwidth and model size
Exponent bits set range; fraction bits set precision
FP32: 1+8+23 bits, used for optimizer states and high precision
FP16: 1+5+10, precise but small range, needs loss scaling
BF16: 1+8+7, FP32-like range at half the size, standard for training
FP8 (E4M3/E5M2) speeds training; INT8/INT4 for inference and QLoRA
cards.formula: Value = (-1)^sign * 1.fraction * 2^(exponent - bias); integer quantization w ~ s * q (s = scaling factor)
cards.example: FP32 is 32 bits (1 sign, 8 exponent, 23 fraction); FP16 is 16 bits (1+5+10); BF16 is 16 bits (1+8+7); FP8 E4M3 is 8 bits (4 exponent, 3 fraction). Lower precision halves or quarters memory, allowing larger batches and longer context.
cards.say: Every number in training has a format. Floating point spends some bits on range and some on precision, and the sweet spot for training is BF sixteen, which keeps a wide range at half the size of full precision.

items.tip: 1 sign + 8 exponent + 23 fraction bits. Used for optimizer states and high precision.
1+5+10. Precise near 1.0 but tiny range, so it needs loss scaling.
1+8+7. Same 8 exponent bits as FP32: wide range at half the size. Standard for training.
E4M3 has 4 exponent and 3 fraction bits. Speeds up training on supported GPUs.
Integers for inference and QLoRA: w ≈ scale x q. INT8 is the bigger sibling.

beats.cap: Every number a model stores has a size in bits, like choosing how many digits to write down.
Some bits set the range, how big or small a number can be, and the rest set the precision.
BF sixteen keeps the wide range of full thirty two bit floats at half the size, so training loves it.
Even smaller formats like eight bits speed up training, and four bit integers help run models cheaply.

cards.title: Why One GPU Is Not Enough
cards.text: A large model simply does not fit on one GPU. A 70B-parameter model needs about 140 GB just for its 16-bit weights, well over the 80 GB of an H100. Gradients, optimizer states and activations add much more memory on top, and activations explode with longer sequences and deeper stacks. The raw compute and the large effective batches needed for stable training would also keep a single GPU busy far too long. The answer is to spread training across many GPUs.
points: 70B params x 2 bytes (BF16) ≈ 140 GB > 80 GB of an H100
Gradients, optimizer states and activations add much more
Activation memory grows with sequence length, depth and width
Total FLOPs too large for one GPU in reasonable time
Solution: distributed training across many GPUs
cards.formula: Weight memory ~ N_params * bytes_per_value  (2 bytes for BF16)
cards.example: 70B parameters at 2 bytes each ≈ 140 GB, versus an H100's 80 GB, so even the weights alone do not fit on one device.
cards.say: A seventy billion parameter model takes about a hundred and forty gigabytes just for its weights in half precision, and one H100 only has eighty. Add gradients and optimizer states and it is hopeless, so training must be spread across many GPUs.
covers: B6: Why single-GPU training is impractical
A6: Why one GPU is not enough and gradient accumulation

items.tip: The memory of a single top training GPU.
70 billion parameters x 2 bytes ≈ 140 GB, for the weights alone.
Rough estimate with 16 bytes per parameter. Activations grow with sequence length, depth and width on top.

beats.cap: Picture trying to pour a big jug of water into one small glass. That is a huge model on one GPU.
A seventy billion parameter model needs about one hundred forty gigabytes just for its weights, but the glass holds eighty.
Gradients, optimizer notes and activations pile on far more, and the compute would take one GPU forever.
The only way out is teamwork: spread the training across many GPUs.

cards.title: Gradient Accumulation
cards.text: Gradient accumulation fakes a large batch when memory only fits a small one. The batch is split into N micro-batches; each gets its own forward and backward pass, and the resulting gradients are summed without touching the weights. Only after all N micro-batches is the averaged gradient applied in a single optimizer step, and the gradient buffer is reset. This keeps peak activation memory low and gives the effect of the full large batch, but because the micro-batches run one after another it does not make training faster.
points: Split a batch into N micro-batches
Forward + backward per micro-batch, accumulate gradients, no update
After N: average gradients, one optimizer step, reset
Enables large effective batches with limited memory
Lowers peak activation memory
Does not speed up training by itself
cards.formula: g_accum = (1/N) * sum_{i=1..N} g_i ; B_eff = N * B_micro
cards.example: N = 8 micro-batches of 256 sequences behave like one batch of 2,048 sequences for the optimizer step, while only 256 sequences ever sit in memory at once.
cards.say: Gradient accumulation lets a small GPU pretend to use a big batch. Each mini batch adds to a running gradient, and only after several of them does the optimizer actually take a step.
covers: A6: Why one GPU is not enough and gradient accumulation

items.tip: Only one micro-batch sits in memory at a time, keeping peak activation memory low.
Compute the gradient for this micro-batch.
Gradients are summed in a buffer. The weights are NOT touched yet.
Average the gradients, update once, reset the buffer. Acts like a 2,048-sequence batch.

beats.cap: Your GPU only fits a small batch, but you want the smooth gradients of a big one. Here is the trick.
Run a small micro batch forward and backward, then add its gradient to a pile without updating anything.
After eight micro batches of two hundred fifty six, average the pile and take one real step.
Memory stays small, but the micro batches run one after another, so it is not any faster.

cards.title: Data Parallelism
cards.text: In data parallelism every GPU keeps a full copy of the model but processes different micro-batches. After the forward and backward passes, gradients are averaged across GPUs so all copies take the same optimizer step and stay identical. It raises throughput and combines naturally with gradient accumulation. The limitation is memory: because parameters, gradients and optimizer states are replicated on every GPU, the model must still fit on a single device, so data parallelism scales speed but not model size.
points: Each GPU holds the full model
Each GPU processes different data
Gradients averaged across GPUs (all-reduce)
Same update on every replica, keeping them in sync
Benefit: higher throughput
Limitation: full model and training states replicated per GPU
cards.formula: B_eff = D * N * B_micro  (D = data-parallel GPUs, N = accumulation steps, B_micro = micro-batch size)
cards.example: With two GPUs, GPU1 processes micro-batches 1 and 3 while GPU2 processes 2 and 4, both holding the full model; their gradients are averaged before both update.
cards.say: Data parallelism gives every GPU the whole model but a different slice of the data. The GPUs average their gradients, so they all update identically and train faster together.
covers: A6: Parallelism strategies: data, tensor, pipeline and 3D

items.tip: Every GPU holds all parameters, gradients and optimizer states.
Identical replica, so the model must still fit on one device.
Each GPU works on different data.
Combines naturally with gradient accumulation.
An all-reduce averages gradients across GPUs.
Both copies take the identical step and stay in sync. Effective batch = GPUs x steps x micro-batch.

beats.cap: Imagine two students with the same textbook, each solving different homework problems to finish faster.
Each GPU holds the whole model but works on different micro batches of data.
Then they average their gradients, so both take the exact same step and stay identical.
This boosts speed, but every GPU still needs the full model, so it cannot train a bigger one.

cards.title: Tensor Parallelism
cards.text: Tensor parallelism splits individual weight matrices across GPUs. A large matrix might be cut into columns, with each GPU multiplying the same input by its own shard to produce a partial output; the partials are then concatenated for an expansion layer or summed for an attention projection. This is applied inside the attention and feed-forward layers when a single layer is too big for one GPU. The price is heavy communication, because the shards exchange partial results frequently during every forward and backward pass.
points: Shard large weight matrices across devices
Each GPU computes a partial result for the same input
Column split -> concatenate; row split -> sum
Applied to attention and feed-forward layers
Handles layers too big for one GPU
Requires frequent, fast GPU-to-GPU communication
cards.formula: Column sharding: W = [W1, W2]; Y = X W = [X W1, X W2], each GPU i computes X Wi
cards.example: A feed-forward weight matrix is split by columns so GPU1 and GPU2 each hold a shard and both process the same micro-batch, then their partial outputs are combined.
cards.say: Tensor parallelism chops a single big weight matrix into pieces across GPUs. Each GPU does only its part, then the pieces are stitched back together. It is powerful but needs constant talking between GPUs.
covers: A6: Parallelism strategies: data, tensor, pipeline and 3D

items.tip: Both GPUs receive the same micro-batch.
W = [W1, W2]: one huge weight matrix cut into shards.
Each GPU computes a partial output with its own shard.
Used inside attention and feed-forward layers that are too big for one GPU.
Column split: concatenate. Row split: sum. Partials are exchanged in every forward and backward pass.

beats.cap: What if a single layer is too big for one GPU? Like a giant pizza, you cut it into slices.
The big weight matrix is split into column slices, and each GPU keeps just one slice.
Both GPUs see the same input, and each computes its own partial answer.
The partial answers are stitched back together, which means the GPUs must talk constantly and quickly.

cards.title: Pipeline Parallelism
cards.text: Pipeline parallelism gives different GPUs different groups of consecutive layers, called stages. A micro-batch flows through the stages in order, and several micro-batches can be in flight at once so the stages all stay busy. This lowers the model memory each GPU must hold and combines well with the other strategies. Its drawbacks are pipeline bubbles, the idle gaps while the pipeline fills and drains, the cost of shipping activations and gradients between stages, and the tricky scheduling of overlapping forward and backward passes.
points: Consecutive layers split into stages on different GPUs
Micro-batches flow through stages, overlapping in time
Reduces model memory per GPU
Combinable with data and tensor parallelism
Pipeline bubbles: idle time during fill and drain
Needs inter-stage communication and careful scheduling
cards.example: GPU1 holds layers 0-3 and GPU2 holds layers 4-6; a micro-batch finishes on GPU1 then moves to GPU2 while the next micro-batch enters GPU1.
cards.say: Pipeline parallelism assigns groups of layers to different GPUs, like stations on an assembly line. Micro batches keep every stage busy, though the first and last stages always waste a little time.
covers: A6: Parallelism strategies: data, tensor, pipeline and 3D

items.tip: Stage 1. Finishes a micro-batch, passes activations on, and starts the next micro-batch.
Stage 2. Receives activations from GPU 1; gradients travel back the other way.
Idle time while the pipeline fills and drains. Scheduling overlapping passes is tricky.

beats.cap: Think of an assembly line where each station does one part of the work, then passes it on.
The first GPU holds the lower layers, the second holds the upper ones, so each needs less memory.
While one micro batch moves up to GPU two, the next one already starts on GPU one.
At the start and end some stations sit idle, little gaps called bubbles, and data must travel between stages.

cards.title: 3D Parallelism and ZeRO
cards.text: Data, tensor and pipeline parallelism can be stacked into 3D parallelism. But plain data parallelism wastefully replicates parameters, gradients and optimizer states on every GPU, and Adam's two moment states alone take several times the parameter memory. ZeRO removes that redundancy by sharding the training states across data-parallel GPUs: stage 1 shards optimizer states, stage 2 also gradients, stage 3 also parameters. It works with all three parallelism types and slashes memory at the cost of more communication. PyTorch's FSDP implements this ZeRO-style sharding, gathering parameters only when needed.
points: 3D parallelism = data + tensor + pipeline together
Plain DP replicates parameters, gradients and optimizer states
Adam stores two moment states, several times the model size
ZeRO stage 1: optimizer states; stage 2: + gradients; stage 3: + parameters
Works with DP, TP, PP; trades memory for communication
PyTorch FSDP: gathers parameters only when needed
cards.formula: Without ZeRO, per GPU ~ (2 + 2 + K) * Psi bytes; ZeRO stage 3 over N_d GPUs ~ (2 + 2 + K) * Psi / N_d
cards.example: ZeRO paper example: a 7.5B model on 64 GPUs (K = 12) drops from a 120 GB per-GPU baseline to 31.4 GB (stage 1), 16.6 GB (stage 2) and just 1.9 GB (stage 3).
cards.say: Plain data parallelism copies the same optimizer states onto every GPU, which is a huge waste. Zero shards those states across GPUs, stage by stage, so memory falls dramatically, from a hundred and twenty gigabytes down to under two.

items.tip: 7.5B model on 64 GPUs: parameters, gradients and Adam states copied on every GPU.
Shard the optimizer states. Adam's two moments take several times the parameter memory.
Also shard the gradients.
Also shard the parameters. PyTorch FSDP does this, gathering parameters only when needed.

beats.cap: Plain data parallelism is like every roommate buying the same fridge full of food. Lots of waste.
Zero shares the load instead: stage one splits the optimizer notes across GPUs.
Stage two also splits the gradients, and stage three splits the weights themselves.
Memory per GPU falls from one hundred twenty gigabytes to under two, paid for with extra communication.

cards.title: Choosing a Strategy
cards.text: Each distributed technique fixes a different bottleneck and brings its own cost. Gradient accumulation buys larger effective batches but lengthens each step. Data parallelism raises throughput but replicates the training states. Tensor parallelism splits oversized layers but communicates constantly. Pipeline parallelism spreads layers across GPUs but creates idle bubbles. ZeRO removes redundant memory but adds coordination. There is no single best choice: large training runs combine several of them to balance memory, speed and communication against the hardware actually available.
points: Larger batches -> gradient accumulation and data parallelism
Layers too large -> tensor parallelism
Model too deep to fit -> pipeline parallelism
Training states too large -> ZeRO
No universally optimal strategy; combine techniques
cards.example: Gradient accumulation trades longer steps for bigger batches; DP trades replicated memory for throughput; TP trades communication for splitting huge layers; PP trades bubbles for less per-GPU memory; ZeRO trades communication for memory.
cards.say: Every strategy solves a different problem and charges a different price. Real training systems mix them together, trading memory, speed and communication to fit the hardware they have.
covers: A6: Parallelism strategies: data, tensor, pipeline and 3D

items.tip: Each technique fixes a different bottleneck and charges a different price.
Gradient accumulation: longer steps. Data parallelism: replicated memory, more speed.
Tensor parallelism: costs constant communication.
Pipeline parallelism: costs idle bubbles.
ZeRO: costs extra coordination.
No single best choice: big runs mix several to match their hardware.

beats.cap: Choosing a strategy is like a doctor picking medicine: first figure out what is actually wrong.
Need bigger batches? Use accumulation or data parallelism. A layer too big? Slice it with tensor parallelism.
A model too deep goes in a pipeline, and oversized training states get sharded with Zero.
Every fix has a cost, so real training runs mix several to balance memory, speed and communication.

cards.title: The Base Model: Llama 3.1 8B
cards.text: The finished product of pretraining is a base model: a network that continues text fluently but has not yet been aligned to follow instructions. Llama 3.1 8B (base) is a decoder-only causal Transformer with about 8 billion parameters, 32 blocks, 4096-dimensional hidden states and 32 attention heads, with a feed-forward size of roughly 14,336 and a context of up to 128k tokens. It was trained by self-supervised next-token prediction on a large multilingual corpus. Its size is set by depth (blocks), width (hidden size), heads and the feed-forward dimension.
points: Pretraining output = base model, not yet instruction-following
Decoder-only causal Transformer
~8B parameters, 32 blocks, hidden size 4096, 32 heads
MLP intermediate size ~14,336
Context up to 128k tokens
Self-supervised next-token prediction on multilingual data
cards.example: Llama 3.1 8B: 32 blocks, d_model 4096, 32 heads, FFN 14,336, 128k context.
cards.say: Pretraining ends with a base model that can continue text well but does not yet follow instructions. Llama three point one eight billion is a decoder only transformer with thirty two layers and a hundred and twenty eight thousand token context.
covers: A6: Result of pretraining: the base model (Llama 3.1 8B)

items.tip: Context of up to 128k tokens.
Each block: 32 attention heads and a feed-forward part of size about 14,336.
32 blocks in total set the depth. Hidden states are 4,096 numbers wide.
Decoder-only and causal: each position only sees earlier tokens.
Trained by self-supervised next-token prediction on a large multilingual corpus. About 8B parameters.

beats.cap: After all that training, what do we actually get? A base model, a brilliant text continuer.
Llama three point one with eight billion parameters stacks thirty two blocks, each four thousand ninety six numbers wide.
Each block has thirty two attention heads, and it can read up to one hundred twenty eight thousand tokens.
It continues text fluently, but it does not follow instructions yet. That comes next.

lessons.title: Training Recipes
lessons.goal: Understand how training recipes schedule data over time and shape capabilities, through multi-stage midtraining, progressive context extension and late-stage domain upsampling.

cards.title: Training Recipes and Scheduling
cards.text: Give two runs the same model, data, token count and compute and they can still end up with different abilities, because how the data is exposed over time matters. A training recipe coordinates the data mixture, the data schedule and the optimization settings across phases. The mixture sets which fraction of tokens comes from each domain; the schedule decides when they appear. The same 30% code share can be spread evenly, concentrated at the start or saved for the end, and each choice hands later gradients a different starting point. Curriculum learning, easy examples first, is a deliberate special case.
points: Same ingredients, different decisions -> different capabilities
Recipe = data schedule plus optimization settings and phases
Mixture = token proportion per domain
Schedule = timing and ordering of data
Order matters: gradients depend on the current weights
Curriculum learning = deliberate easy-to-hard progression
cards.example: Three schedules all use 30% code overall: uniform (30% throughout), early (60% in the first half, 0% after) and late (0% first, then 60% in the second half). Same budget, different skills.
cards.say: Two runs can share the same data and budget yet end up different, because when the model sees each domain matters. A recipe decides the mixture and the timing of everything the model reads.
covers: B6: Training recipes and data scheduling

items.tip: Same model, data, tokens and compute can still give different abilities.
Which share of tokens comes from each domain, like 30% code overall.
When each domain appears. Order matters because gradients depend on the current weights.
Learning rate and other settings, coordinated across training phases.
Code spread evenly from start to finish.
All code in the first half.
All code saved for the second half. Curriculum learning, easy to hard, is a deliberate schedule too.

beats.cap: Two cooks with the same ingredients can still bake very different cakes. Training models works the same way.
A recipe decides the mixture, how much of each kind of text, plus the timing and the optimizer settings.
Thirty percent code can be spread evenly, packed at the start, or saved for the end.
Each choice gives later learning a different starting point, so the same budget yields different skills.

cards.title: OLMo 2: Multi-Stage Training
cards.text: OLMo 2 7B shows how recipes work in stages. Stage 1 is broad pretraining on about 4 trillion tokens. Stage 2, called midtraining, continues next-token prediction for 50 billion tokens on Dolmino Mix, a curated blend of high-quality web, math and question-answering data. This is repeated three times from the same checkpoint with different data shuffles, and the three resulting models are averaged element-wise. The learning rate warms up and decays during broad pretraining, then gets a final annealing on the targeted data, letting the model refine itself without overwriting earlier skills. Weight averaging adds stability at no extra inference cost.
points: Multi-stage: successive phases with different data or settings
Midtraining = continued pretraining with the same objective
Stage 1: ~4T tokens of broad pretraining
Stage 2: 3 x 50B tokens on Dolmino Mix, different shuffles
Final model = element-wise average of the three runs
High-quality data paired with decreasing LR (final annealing)
cards.formula: theta_final = (theta_A + theta_B + theta_C) / 3  (element-wise weight averaging)
cards.example: OLMo 2 7B: stage 1 about 4T tokens, then three continuations of 50B tokens each (shuffles A, B, C), averaged into one final model.
cards.say: OLMo two trains in stages. It first reads four trillion tokens broadly, then does a targeted midtraining pass on curated math and question answering, three times over, and averages the three results into one stronger model.
covers: B6: OLMo 2: multi-stage training and weight averaging

items.tip: Stage 1: wide pretraining, learning rate warms up and decays.
Stage 2: same next-token objective on Dolmino Mix: curated web, math and Q&A data, with a final annealing.
Three runs from the same checkpoint with different data orders.
theta_final = average of A, B and C, element by element. More stability, no extra inference cost.
Refined on targeted data without overwriting earlier skills.

beats.cap: Like school then a focused exam prep course, OLMo two learns in stages.
First it reads about four trillion tokens of broad text to learn the basics.
Then it studies fifty billion tokens of hand picked math, quality web and question answering, as the learning rate gently winds down.
That prep is done three times with different shuffles, and the three models are averaged into one.

cards.title: Extending the Context (Llama 3)
cards.text: Llama 3 was first pretrained with an 8K-token context window, then stretched to 128K tokens in six progressive stages of continued next-token prediction using about 800 billion extra tokens. Long sequences are added late because attention compute grows quadratically with length, so short-context training is far cheaper. The model only moves to the next length after it recovers its short-context performance and passes needle-in-a-haystack tests, which check that it can still find a fact buried in a long document. The objective never changes; only the sequence length does.
points: Start: 8K context; target: 128K context
Six progressive stages of increasing sequence length
~800B additional tokens for the extension
Same next-token objective on longer sequences
Long sequences come late because attention cost is quadratic
Advance only when short-context and needle tests pass
cards.example: 8K -> 128K context in six stages using roughly 800B extra tokens, each stage gated by short-context recovery and needle-in-a-haystack checks.
cards.say: Llama three started with an eight thousand token context and grew it to a hundred and twenty eight thousand in six stages, adding about eight hundred billion tokens. Long sequences come last because attention gets expensive fast.

items.tip: Llama 3 is first pretrained with an 8,000-token context: cheap and fast.
Each stage only advances after short-context skills recover and needle-in-a-haystack tests pass.
Reached with about 800B extra tokens. The next-token objective never changes.

beats.cap: Reading a whole book at once is expensive, so Llama three first practiced on shorter passages.
It started with eight thousand tokens, because attention cost grows with the square of the length.
Then it climbed in six steps, and only moved up after passing tests that hide one fact in a long document.
With about eight hundred billion extra tokens, it reached one hundred twenty eight thousand tokens.

cards.title: Late-Stage Domain Upsampling
cards.text: Domain upsampling raises the sampling probability of chosen domains above their original share. In a controlled test with a 7B model and 1 trillion tokens, upsampling selected domains during only the final 20% of training improved math and code benchmarks over the original mixture, without adding any tokens. The gains were not free everywhere: MMLU rose from 35.69 to 42.59, GSM8K from 14.71 to 22.97 and HumanEval from 17.23 to 23.40, while a language-understanding score slipped slightly from 61.52 to 60.08. Changing the schedule shifts capabilities rather than lifting everything.
points: Domain upsampling: raise the sampling probability of chosen domains
Setup: 7B model, 1T tokens, same budget
Upsampling only in the final 20% of training
Math (GSM8K) and code (HumanEval) improve clearly
Language understanding drops slightly
Capabilities shift without more tokens
cards.example: No upsampling vs final-20% upsampling: MMLU 35.69 -> 42.59, GSM8K 14.71 -> 22.97, HumanEval 17.23 -> 23.40, while language understanding eased from 61.52 to 60.08.
cards.say: If you feed more math and code in the last fifth of training, the model gets much better at those, with no extra tokens. But language understanding dips a little, so you are trading skills, not adding them for free.

items.tip: General knowledge quiz. 7B model, 1T tokens.
Up almost 7 points, with no extra tokens.
Grade-school math word problems.
Math improves clearly.
Writing working Python functions.
Code improves clearly.
A language-understanding score.
Slips slightly: capabilities shift rather than all rising.

beats.cap: What if, in the last stretch of training, you served the model extra helpings of math and code?
In a test with a seven billion model and one trillion tokens, only the final fifth was changed.
Math jumped from about fifteen to twenty three, and code from about seventeen to twenty three, with no extra tokens.
But language understanding dipped a little, so you are trading skills rather than getting them free.

lessons.title: Scaling Laws
lessons.goal: Understand how held-out loss falls predictably with model size, data and compute, and how scaling laws guide budget, allocation and deployment choices.

cards.title: What Scaling Laws Are
cards.text: Scaling laws are empirical formulas describing how a model's held-out prediction loss changes with its size, its training data and its training compute. They turn a fixed budget into a plan: build a bigger model on fewer tokens, or a smaller model on more tokens? In practice, larger and better-trained models reach lower loss, but with diminishing returns. Each multiplicative step in scale buys a roughly constant percentage improvement rather than a fixed amount. Because the pattern is smooth, small runs let you forecast large ones, but only inside the range you actually measured.
points: Resources: model size N, training tokens D, compute C, held-out loss L
Goal: find the allocation that minimizes loss for a budget
Larger, sufficiently trained models reach lower held-out loss
Diminishing returns: a constant relative gain per scaling step
Power law: constant percentage improvement per multiplicative scale-up
Fits are reliable only within the range of conditions measured
cards.formula: L(X) ~ (X_c / X)^alpha  (X = size, tokens or compute; X_c and alpha are fitted constants)
cards.example: Training runs of many sizes fall on a straight line on a log-log plot of loss against scale. Extrapolating that line forecasts the loss of a model far larger than any you actually trained.
cards.say: Scaling laws say that as you grow a model, its data or its compute, the prediction error falls smoothly and predictably, following a power law. That lets engineers forecast how a large model will do before paying to train it.
covers: A7: What scaling laws are and why they matter

items.tip: Cheap experiments at small scale. Loss is measured on held-out text the model never trained on.
On a log-log plot, runs of many sizes line up on a nearly straight line.
Extend the fitted line to predict a much bigger model. Only safe inside the measured range.

beats.cap: Imagine a fixed budget: should you build a bigger model on less text, or a smaller one on more?
Scaling laws answer that by measuring how loss falls as size, data and compute grow.
Each time you multiply the scale, loss drops by roughly the same percentage, so returns slowly shrink.
The pattern is so smooth that small runs can forecast big ones, but only within the range you measured.

cards.title: Kaplan's Power Law
cards.text: In 2020 Kaplan and colleagues measured held-out loss for language models of many sizes and found that, for sufficiently trained models, loss follows a power law in the number of non-embedding parameters. The exponent is small, about 0.076, so doubling the model multiplies loss by roughly 0.949, about five percent lower. Loss bends toward an irreducible floor, the entropy of natural language, that no model can beat. Such tiny exponents mean returns diminish, yet improvement persists across many orders of magnitude. But Kaplan used fixed data and training settings, which overestimated how large models should be.
points: Loss vs non-embedding parameter count follows a power law
Exponent alpha_N estimated at about 0.076
Doubling model size -> multiply loss by 2^-0.076 ~ 0.949 (~5.1% lower)
Irreducible loss floor = entropy of natural language
Exponents around 0.05-0.1: diminishing but persistent returns
Flaw: fixed settings overestimated the optimal model size
cards.example: Doubling model size cuts loss by about 5.1%. Kaplan's implied recipe grew the model about 5.5x and the data only about 1.8x for 10x compute, which later turned out to starve big models of tokens.
cards.say: Kaplan's team found that bigger models lose error following a power law with a small exponent, so doubling the size cuts loss by only about five percent. Their fit assumed fixed data, which later turned out to overestimate how big models should be.

items.tip: Starting loss, shown as 100 percent. Kaplan counted non-embedding parameters.
Loss times 2 to the power minus 0.076, about 0.949: roughly 5.1 percent lower.
Another doubling, another five percent off. The exponent 0.076 is tiny.
Gains persist across many orders of magnitude but bend toward a floor: the entropy of language.

beats.cap: In 2020, Kaplan and colleagues trained models of many sizes and watched how their loss changed.
Doubling the model shaved off only about five percent of the loss, every single time.
Keep doubling and loss keeps falling, but toward a floor no model can beat, the natural messiness of language.
Because the data and settings stayed fixed, this recipe told people to build models that were too big.

cards.title: Training Compute C = 6ND
cards.text: For a dense Transformer, where every parameter is used for every token, the total training compute is approximately six times the number of parameters times the number of training tokens. The factor six comes from about two floating-point operations per parameter per token in the forward pass and about four in the backward pass, ignoring extra costs such as attention overhead. The formula makes budget trade-offs concrete: doubling the tokens at a fixed size doubles compute, while halving the model and doubling the tokens leaves compute unchanged. Under a fixed budget, a larger model must therefore see fewer tokens.
points: Dense Transformers use all parameters for every token
Training compute C ~ 6 N D
About 2 FLOPs per parameter per token forward, about 4 backward
Excludes extra operations such as attention overhead
Fixed C: a bigger model N must take smaller D
cards.formula: C ~ 6 N D  (C = training FLOPs, N = parameters, D = training tokens)
cards.example: N = 2B parameters on D = 40B tokens is 1x compute; 2B on 80B tokens is 2x; 1B on 80B tokens is back to 1x. Halving the model and doubling the tokens keeps the training budget constant.
cards.say: Total training compute is about six times the parameter count times the token count, roughly two operations per parameter per token forward and four backward. So with a fixed budget, a bigger model can only see fewer tokens.

items.tip: 6 times 2 billion times 40 billion: our baseline budget.
Same model, twice the tokens: twice the compute.
Half the model, twice the tokens: back to the same budget.

beats.cap: Training cost has a surprisingly simple recipe: six, times the number of parameters, times the number of tokens.
The six comes from about two operations per parameter going forward and four coming back, for every token.
Feed the same two billion parameter model twice the tokens, and the bill doubles.
Halve the model and double the tokens, and the cost is unchanged, so bigger models must see fewer tokens.

cards.title: Chinchilla: Scale Both Equally
cards.text: DeepMind's Chinchilla study re-examined scaling by training more than 400 models from 70M to 16B parameters on 5B to 500B tokens, matching the learning-rate schedule to each run length. Plotting loss against model size at a fixed compute budget gives a U-shaped IsoFLOP curve: left of the minimum the model is too small, right of it the model is too large and undertrained. Joining the minima shows that parameters and tokens should grow roughly equally with compute. This corrected Kaplan's advice and revealed that many earlier large models carried too many parameters for their token count.
points: IsoFLOP curve: loss vs model size at constant compute
Left of the minimum: too small; right: too few tokens
Optimum shifts to larger models and lower loss as compute grows
N_opt ~ C^0.49, D_opt ~ C^0.51: scale both about equally
Kaplan grew parameters much faster than tokens
Many earlier models were undertrained for their size
cards.formula: N_opt ~ C^0.49 ; D_opt ~ C^0.51
cards.example: For 10x compute, Chinchilla grows the model 3.09x and the tokens 3.24x, while Kaplan's older fit grew the model 5.37x but the tokens only 1.86x. GPT-3 (175B parameters, ~300B tokens) was undertrained and should have seen 3-4 trillion tokens.
cards.say: Chinchilla trained hundreds of models and found that parameters and data should grow together: ten times the compute means about three times the model and three times the data. That showed earlier giants like GPT-3 were starved of tokens.

items.tip: Plenty of tokens, but the model lacks capacity to use them.
The compute-optimal size. With more compute it moves to bigger models and lower loss.
Too many parameters for the budget, so it sees too few tokens and stays undertrained.

beats.cap: Picture a fixed amount of compute and a dial for model size. Where should you set it?
DeepMind trained over four hundred models and found a valley: too small on one side, too big on the other.
Joining the valley floors for bigger budgets shows that model size and data should grow about equally.
For ten times the compute, grow the model about three times and the tokens about three times too.
So GPT-3, with three hundred billion tokens, was undertrained and should have seen three to four trillion.

cards.title: ~20 Tokens per Parameter
cards.text: Chinchilla itself, with 70 billion parameters trained on about 1.4 trillion tokens, illustrates a handy rule of thumb: about twenty training tokens per parameter is compute-optimal. Its predecessor Gopher had 280 billion parameters but only about 300 billion tokens, roughly one token per parameter, and was heavily undertrained for its size. At roughly the same training compute, Chinchilla used four times fewer parameters and about 4.7 times more tokens, and it outperformed Gopher on a wide range of downstream evaluations.
points: Compute-optimal is roughly 20 training tokens per parameter
Chinchilla: 70B parameters, 1.4T tokens
Gopher: 280B parameters, ~300B tokens (~1.1 tokens/parameter)
Same compute; Chinchilla scored better on many evaluations
4x fewer parameters, about 4.7x more tokens
cards.formula: D_opt ~ 20 * N  (rule of thumb)
cards.example: Gopher (2021): 280B parameters on ~300B tokens, about 1.1 tokens per parameter. Chinchilla (2022): 70B parameters on 1,400B tokens, 20 tokens per parameter. About equal compute, but Chinchilla won on many benchmarks.
cards.say: The rule of thumb from Chinchilla is about twenty training tokens for every parameter. Chinchilla had seventy billion parameters and far more tokens than the much larger Gopher, yet it scored better at similar compute.
covers: B6: Chinchilla rule of thumb: ~20 tokens per parameter

items.tip: Gopher, 2021: 280 billion parameters.
Only about 300 billion tokens, roughly 1.1 tokens per parameter: heavily undertrained.
Chinchilla, 2022: 70 billion parameters, four times fewer than Gopher.
1.4 trillion tokens, about 4.7 times more than Gopher and 20 per parameter.

beats.cap: Here is a handy kitchen rule for training: about twenty tokens of text for every parameter.
Gopher was huge, with two hundred eighty billion parameters, but saw only about one token per parameter.
Chinchilla used four times fewer parameters but almost five times more tokens, on roughly the same compute.
The smaller, better fed Chinchilla beat Gopher on many tests, proving the rule in practice.

cards.title: Overtraining & Deploy-Optimal
cards.text: Compute-optimal training minimizes loss for a fixed training budget, but a deployed model also pays for every request it serves. Overtraining means training a model on more tokens than the Chinchilla-optimal amount for its size, spending more on training so that a smaller, cheaper model reaches the required quality. This differs from overfitting: with overtraining, held-out loss can keep improving. A simple lifetime-cost model adds the one-time training cost to the number of requests times the per-request inference cost, and the break-even point decides which model is cheaper in the end.
points: Compute-optimal: minimize loss per training budget
Deployment-optimal: meet quality at minimum lifetime cost
Overtraining = more tokens than compute-optimal for its size
Smaller model means lower inference memory and cost
Overtraining is not overfitting
The cheaper model depends on the number of requests
cards.formula: C_total = C_train + R * c_inf  (C_train = one-time training cost, R = requests, c_inf = cost per request); break-even R* = (C_train,B - C_train,A) / (c_inf,A - c_inf,B)
cards.example: Model A (larger): training EUR 200,000, inference EUR 0.002 per request. Model B (smaller, overtrained): EUR 300,000, EUR 0.001 per request. At 100M requests they tie; below that A is cheaper, above it B wins - at 200M, A costs EUR 600,000 versus B's EUR 500,000.
cards.say: Deployed models cost money on every request, so it often pays to overtrain a smaller model: spend more once so each answer is cheaper forever. Whether that wins depends on how many requests you actually serve.

items.tip: Compute-optimal training for its size: cheaper to train.
Overtrained: more tokens than compute-optimal, so training costs more.
A bigger model needs more memory and compute for every answer.
Half the serving cost per request.
200,000 plus 200 million times 0.002.
300,000 plus 200 million times 0.001. They tie at exactly 100 million requests.

beats.cap: Training is a one-time bill, but a deployed model pays again for every single answer it serves.
Overtraining means feeding a smaller model extra tokens, paying more up front so it is cheaper to run.
At one hundred million requests both cost the same, and beyond that the smaller model wins.
And do not confuse it with overfitting, because with overtraining the held-out loss can keep improving.

cards.title: Limits & Practical Use
cards.text: Scaling laws are fitted to specific experiments and can fail when conditions change. Better data quality can lower loss without adding tokens, repeated data counts toward compute but brings little new information, mixture-of-experts and other architectures follow different curves, and optimizer or schedule choices shift the observed loss. Extrapolating far beyond the fitted range is risky. In practice engineers run small experiments, fit a scaling relation, validate it with a larger pilot run, then choose the deployed model on task quality, memory, latency and lifetime cost - not on training loss alone.
points: Data quality and repetition change the relationship
Dense and mixture-of-experts models scale differently
The training recipe affects the observed loss
Extrapolation becomes unreliable far from the fitted range
Workflow: small runs -> fit -> pilot validation -> deployment choice
Final choice uses quality, memory, latency and lifetime cost
cards.example: A law fitted on dense Transformers cannot be trusted to predict a mixture-of-experts model trained on heavily repeated data.
cards.say: Scaling laws are only as good as the experiments behind them. Better data, repeated tokens, new architectures and different recipes all break the fit, so engineers run small tests, then a pilot, and pick the deployed model on task quality and cost.
covers: B6: Limits and practical use of scaling laws

items.tip: Cheap experiments with your own data, architecture and recipe.
Data quality, repeated data, mixture-of-experts and the optimizer all change the curve.
A larger test run checks the forecast before you spend the big budget.
Judge on task quality, memory, latency and lifetime cost, not training loss alone.

beats.cap: A scaling law is like a weather forecast: great nearby, shaky far ahead, and tied to local conditions.
Change the data quality, repeat data, or switch to mixture of experts, and the old curve may not fit.
So engineers fit a law on small runs, then check it with a bigger pilot before committing.
The final model is chosen on quality, memory, speed and lifetime cost, not training loss alone.

lessons.title: In-Context Learning
lessons.goal: Understand how a model learns tasks from prompt examples without weight updates, why that ability emerges from pretraining, and where it breaks down.

cards.title: In-Context Learning
cards.text: In-context learning is the model's ability to pick up a new task at inference time from examples written in the prompt, with no change to its weights. It emerges naturally from large-scale next-token training: the model spots the pattern in the input and adapts its internal hidden states to match it. Because nothing is learned permanently, the same model can switch between translation, sorting or classification just by being shown the right examples. This is what lets a single model serve countless tasks without ever being retrained.
points: ICL: learn a task from prompt examples with no parameter updates
Emerges from next-token prediction at scale
Model adapts its hidden-state dynamics to the pattern
Works for translation, sorting, classification and more
Nothing is stored in the weights; the task lives in the context
cards.example: Show the model 'English: cat -> German: Katze' and it can translate a new word it was never explicitly trained to translate, simply by following the pattern in the prompt.
cards.say: In-context learning is the model picking up a new task just from examples in the prompt, without changing any weights. It comes out of large-scale next-token training, and it lets one model do many tasks on demand.
covers: A6: What in-context learning is and base-model behaviour

items.tip: An example written right into the prompt. No training run, no weight change.
A second example makes the pattern crystal clear.
A new word the model was never explicitly taught to translate this way.
The model adapts its hidden states to the pattern. Its weights stay exactly the same.

beats.cap: Imagine learning a card game just by watching two rounds, without anyone explaining the rules.
You write a couple of examples straight into the prompt, like cat becomes Katze and dog becomes Hund.
The model spots the pattern and answers Haus, even though none of its weights changed.
This skill grew out of huge next-word training, and it lets one model switch tasks on demand.

cards.title: Base Models Just Continue
cards.text: A base model - the raw result of pretraining - has no instruction-following behavior; it only continues text in a statistically likely way. Ask it to plan a Paris trip and it rambles on with an invented itinerary full of blog-style sections rather than answering. Type 'translate Blume from German to English' and it echoes the phrase and lists related compound words instead of giving a translation. This continuation habit is why bare base models feel unusable as assistants, and why alignment matters.
points: A base model continues text, it does not answer questions
Paris prompt -> long invented travel narrative with blog-style sections
'translate Blume' -> repeats the phrase and related compound words
It imitates the expected genre, not the user's intent
A direct consequence of next-token training on raw web text
cards.example: Prompt 'I am going to have breakfast at' -> an invented travel story full of made-up facts. Prompt 'translate Blume from German to English' -> 'translate blume into english...', Blumensprudler, Blumenkistchen.
cards.say: A base model does not answer you, it just continues whatever you type. Ask it about Paris and it writes an invented blog post; ask it to translate a word and it echoes the prompt and lists related words.
covers: A6: What in-context learning is and base-model behaviour

items.tip: You hoped for a helpful, direct answer to your request.
It rambles on with blog-style sections and made-up facts, because that text is likely online.
A one-word translation would have been perfect.
It repeats translate blume into english and lists compounds like Blumenkistchen.

beats.cap: A base model is like a friend who finishes your sentences but never actually answers your question.
Ask it to plan a Paris trip, and it spins an invented travel blog instead of a plan.
Ask it to translate Blume, and it echoes your words and lists related German compound words.
It copies the style of text it saw online, not what you meant, which is why alignment matters.

cards.title: Few-Shot Prompting
cards.text: When the prompt contains a clear pattern of examples, a base model can produce exactly the output you want. Listing German-to-English word pairs and ending with 'Blume ->' makes the model output just 'flower', because every example ended with a single English word and nothing else. Two input/output examples of turning key-value text into JSON lead it to format a third correctly. The model is not following instructions like a human; it predicts the most probable continuation of the pattern, so the example format constrains the answer's format.
points: Consistent example pairs define the task
The example format constrains the output format
Strong structural cues give clean, minimal answers
The same mechanism produces structured output like JSON
It is pattern continuation, not true instruction following
cards.example: Milch -> milk, Butter -> butter, Fenster -> window, Blume -> flower. Or: 'name=Clara, age=32, city=Hamburg' -> {"name": "Clara", "age": 32, "city": "Hamburg"} after two similar examples.
cards.say: Give the model a few clean examples and it copies the pattern exactly. A list of German words with English translations makes it answer with one English word, and two JSON examples make it format a third correctly.
covers: A6: Few-shot prompting examples: translation and JSON

scene.text: Milch -> milk, Butter -> butter, Fenster -> window, Blume -> flower

items.tip: Example one: a German word, an arrow, one English word.
Example two keeps exactly the same format.
Example three. Consistent pairs define the task.
The open slot. The pattern makes a single English word the most likely next thing.
The same trick works for JSON: two key-value to JSON examples make it format a third correctly.

beats.cap: Want a clean answer from a base model? Show it a few tidy examples, like a fill in the blank worksheet.
Each line is a German word, an arrow and exactly one English word, nothing more.
End with Blume and an arrow, and the most likely continuation is simply flower.
It is not obeying instructions like a person, it is just continuing the pattern you set up.

cards.title: Algorithmic vs Semantic ICL
cards.text: Researchers split in-context learning into two modes. Algorithmic ICL covers mechanical skills such as copying, sorting or completing a repeated sequence; it comes from the structure of self-attention plus large-scale training. Semantic ICL uses the model's stored world knowledge to infer what a task means, such as working out that a set of examples describes English-to-German translation. Together the two modes enable few-shot and zero-shot behaviour. The distinction matters because algorithmic skills are about pattern-matching inside the prompt, while semantic skills lean on knowledge baked into the weights.
points: Algorithmic ICL: copying, sorting, repeating patterns, matching prefixes
Semantic ICL: task inference using latent world knowledge
Algorithmic comes from self-attention and scale
Semantic uses knowledge stored during pretraining
Together they enable few-shot and zero-shot learning
cards.example: Algorithmic: 'A B C ... A B ?' -> C. Semantic: 'English cat -> German Katze; dog -> Hund' lets the model infer the translation task and handle a new word.
cards.say: In-context learning has two flavours. Algorithmic learning handles mechanical patterns like copying or completing a sequence, while semantic learning figures out the task from stored knowledge, like realising a list of word pairs is a translation task.
covers: A6: Modes of ICL, why it emerges, and its limits

items.tip: Together the two modes make few-shot and zero-shot behaviour possible.
Mechanical skills that come from the structure of self-attention plus large-scale training.
Task inference that leans on world knowledge stored in the weights during pretraining.
Copying, sorting, repeating patterns and matching prefixes inside the prompt.

items.l: A B C A B ? -> C
items.tip: Completing a repeated sequence needs no knowledge of what the letters mean.
Working out what a set of examples is asking for.
The model realises this is English to German translation and can handle a new word.

beats.cap: Learning from examples comes in two flavours, a bit like a parrot and a detective.
The algorithmic flavour does mechanical jobs, like copying, sorting or finishing a repeated pattern of letters.
The semantic flavour uses what the model knows about the world to work out what the task even is.
One is pattern matching inside the prompt, the other leans on knowledge baked into the weights.

cards.title: Induction Heads
cards.text: In-context learning emerges because training text is full of example-solution and question-answer patterns, so the model implicitly learns to learn. At scale, specific attention circuits called induction heads appear: they look back for an earlier occurrence of the current token and copy whatever followed it. That is the mechanism behind algorithmic ICL - completing 'A B C ... A B' with 'C' because the head finds the earlier 'A B' and copies its successor. Self-attention and positional encodings let the model locate such patterns inside the prompt.
points: Training text is full of example-answer patterns
The model implicitly learns to learn from them
Induction heads form at scale and drive algorithmic ICL
They find an earlier match and copy the token that followed
Self-attention plus positional encoding make this possible
cards.example: Given 'A B C A B ?', an induction head notices the earlier 'A B' and copies the token that came after it, 'C'.
cards.say: The ability to learn from examples emerges because training text is full of patterns. At scale the model grows induction heads, attention circuits that find an earlier match and copy whatever came next, which is how it completes sequences.
covers: A6: Modes of ICL, why it emerges, and its limits

items.tip: First time A appears.
First time B appears, right after A.
The token that followed the earlier A B. This is what gets copied.
The pattern starts repeating.
The current token. The head searches for where B appeared before.
The prediction slot: the head copies C here.

beats.cap: Training text is packed with question and answer patterns, so the model quietly learns how to learn.
At scale, special attention circuits appear, called induction heads, that act like a find and copy tool.
Standing on the second B, the head looks back to the earlier B and grabs what came next.
So it predicts C, and self-attention plus position information make this search possible.

cards.title: Limits of ICL
cards.text: In-context learning is still statistical continuation, not reasoning with guarantees. It is sensitive to the format, order and quality of the examples: the same task can succeed or fail depending on how the prompt is laid out, and a bad example can mislead the model. It offers no guarantee of correctness or safety, and a model may simply ignore the instructions or examples and follow a more familiar pattern from its training. So ICL is powerful and cheap, but it must be measured and checked rather than trusted blindly.
points: ICL is statistical continuation, not guaranteed reasoning
Sensitive to formatting, ordering and example quality
A misleading example can steer the answer wrong
No guarantee of correctness or safety
The model may ignore the prompt and follow a training pattern
cards.example: The same word-pair task gives a clean one-word answer with tidy examples but rambling text when the examples are inconsistent or their order confuses the pattern.
cards.say: In-context learning is still just pattern continuation. It is picky about formatting and example quality, gives no guarantee of being correct or safe, and the model may even ignore your prompt and follow a habit from training.
covers: A6: Modes of ICL, why it emerges, and its limits

items.tip: Same format on every line gives a clean one-word answer.
Mixed formats or a confusing order can lead to rambling text.
Good examples steer the model toward the right pattern.
A single misleading example can steer the answer wrong.
Still no guarantee of correctness or safety: it is statistical continuation.
The model may ignore your prompt and follow a more familiar pattern from training.

beats.cap: Learning from examples feels like magic, but it is still just clever pattern continuation, not careful reasoning.
The same task can succeed or fail depending on the layout, order and quality of your examples.
Even a tidy prompt gives no guarantee of a correct or safe answer, and old habits can win.
So enjoy how cheap and powerful it is, but always measure and check the results.

lessons.title: Alignment: SFT
lessons.goal: Understand why models are post-trained after pretraining, how supervised fine-tuning turns a base model into an assistant, and where imitation alone falls short.

cards.title: Pretraining then Post-Training
cards.text: Modern LLMs are trained in two stages. Pretraining gives the model broad knowledge of language, facts and reasoning patterns from huge text corpora, producing a capable base model that is not yet aligned with human intentions. Post-training then shapes that raw ability into helpful, instruction-following, safe behavior that reflects human preferences. The stages are kept separate because pretraining is extremely expensive and done once, while alignment is cheap enough to iterate and gives clearer control without destroying the pretrained knowledge.
points: Stage 1 pretraining: grammar, semantics, world knowledge, general representations
Result: a powerful base model that is not aligned or instruction-following
Stage 2 post-training: follow instructions, behave helpfully and appropriately
Post-training reduces harmful, biased or unsafe behaviour and encodes preferences
Pretraining is expensive and done once; alignment is cheaper and iterated
The split avoids catastrophic deviation from pretrained knowledge
cards.example: A base model that knows grammar and world facts will still ramble; post-training turns the same weights into an assistant that answers, summarises and refuses unsafe requests.
cards.say: Models are built in two stages. Pretraining soaks up language and knowledge from huge text corpora and leaves a capable but unruly base model; post-training then shapes that raw ability into a helpful, safe assistant. The split keeps the expensive step fixed while alignment stays cheap to iterate.

items.tip: Books, web pages and code: the raw material for learning language.
Learns grammar, meaning, world facts and general representations. Very expensive, done once.
Powerful but not aligned: it rambles instead of following instructions.
Cheap enough to iterate. Encodes preferences and reduces harmful, biased or unsafe behaviour.
Same weights, now answering, summarising and refusing unsafe requests.

beats.cap: Think of a brilliant student who has read every book but has never learned how to hold a conversation.
Pretraining soaks up language and world knowledge from huge piles of text, leaving a capable but unruly base model.
