Token value in this dimension.
Average: 0.3, 0.8, 0.4, 0.2, 0.6 add to 2.3, divided by 5 gives 0.46. Stable, the usual default.
Biggest value per dimension. Highlights standout features but can be noisy.
Simply takes the final vector of the first special token as the summary.

beats.cap: BERT gives every word its own vector, like five separate opinions, but we want one opinion for the whole sentence.
Here is just one number from each token's vector. Pooling squeezes them into a single value per dimension.
Mean pooling simply averages them, giving about zero point four six. It is calm, stable and most common.
Max pooling keeps the biggest value, while CLS pooling just trusts the special first token.
Sentence BERT is BERT fine tuned on sentence pairs plus this pooling step, ready for fast semantic search.

cards.title: Siamese Bi-Encoder Training
cards.text: Sentence-BERT is trained by starting from a pretrained BERT encoder and feeding it pairs of sentences that are either semantically similar or dissimilar. Each sentence passes independently through the same BERT with shared weights, a siamese or bi-encoder setup, followed by pooling. The two resulting vectors are compared with cosine similarity, and a contrastive loss pulls similar pairs together and pushes dissimilar pairs apart. The goal is correct relative distances rather than hitting exact similarity scores. Because sentences are encoded independently, document embeddings can be precomputed.
points: Initialize from a pretrained BERT encoder
Train on similar and dissimilar sentence pairs
Both sentences use the same encoder with shared parameters (siamese/bi-encoder)
Pooling yields one vector per sentence
Contrastive loss pulls similar pairs together and pushes dissimilar pairs apart
Independent encoding means document embeddings can be precomputed
cards.formula: cos_sim(u, v) = (u . v) / (||u|| ||v||), between pooled sentence vectors u and v
cards.example: A similar pair such as two paraphrases has its two vectors pulled together, while an unrelated pair is pushed apart; only their relative distance matters, not the exact cosine value.
cards.say: Sentence-BERT is trained with two identical towers that share their weights. Each sentence goes through its own tower, and a contrastive loss pulls the vectors of similar sentences together and pushes dissimilar ones apart. Because the towers are separate, documents can be encoded ahead of time.

items.tip: Either similar, like two paraphrases, or dissimilar. Training starts from a pretrained BERT.
Siamese or bi-encoder: both sentences go through one encoder with shared weights, separately.
Pooling gives one vector per sentence, called u and v.
Dot product of u and v divided by the product of their lengths.
Pulls similar pairs together, pushes dissimilar pairs apart. Relative distance matters, not exact values.

beats.cap: Think of twins wearing identical glasses: they look at two different sentences in exactly the same way.
Each sentence runs through the same BERT on its own, then pooling turns it into one vector.
The two vectors are compared with cosine similarity, which measures how much they point the same way.
The loss pulls paraphrases together and pushes unrelated pairs apart. Getting the order right matters, not exact scores.
Because each text is encoded alone, all documents can be embedded ahead of time and stored.

cards.title: Embedding Model Types
cards.text: General-purpose Sentence-BERT-style models are trained on broad web-scale data, giving strong zero-shot semantic understanding for open-domain QA and assistants, but they can miss specialized terminology and larger models cost more latency. Domain-adapted models are fine-tuned on narrow corpora such as legal, medical or code text, improving recall inside that domain at the cost of weaker generalization. Cross-lingual models share one embedding space across languages, so a query in one language can retrieve documents in another, with slightly weaker monolingual performance. Newer trends include instruction-tuned and asymmetric encoders.
points: General-purpose: broad data, strong zero-shot, may miss domain jargon
Domain-adapted: fine-tuned on legal, medical or code; higher in-domain recall
Domain use cases: enterprise RAG, scientific literature, technical docs
Cross-lingual: one shared multilingual space via parallel, translation and NLI data
Cross-lingual lets a query in one language retrieve documents in another
Newer trends: instruction-tuned encoders, joint training with LLMs, asymmetric query/document encoders
cards.example: A German query retrieves English documents in a cross-lingual model, while a legal term is clustered with the right documents only in a domain-adapted legal model.
cards.say: Not every task wants the same embedder. General models handle everyday language well, domain-adapted ones know legal or medical jargon, and cross-lingual ones line up several languages in one space so a question can find answers written in another language.

items.tip: Choosing one is like choosing which kind of expert reads your documents.
Sentence-BERT style, trained on broad web data. Bigger ones cost more latency.
Fine-tuned on narrow text like legal, medical or code. Weaker outside its domain.
Trained with parallel, translation and NLI data. Slightly weaker in a single language.
Good for open-domain QA and assistants, but may miss specialist jargon.
Higher recall in-domain: enterprise RAG, scientific papers, technical docs.
One shared space for all languages, so a query in one finds documents in another.
Instruction-tuned encoders, joint training with LLMs, separate query and document encoders.

beats.cap: Embedding models are like doctors: there are general practitioners and specialists, and you pick the right one for the job.
General models learned from the whole web, so they understand almost anything out of the box but can miss jargon.
Domain models are fine tuned on legal, medical or code text, so a legal term finds the right documents.
Cross lingual models share one space for many languages, so a German question can find English documents.
Newer encoders follow instructions or treat questions and documents differently. Every gain in focus costs some generality.

lessons.title: Chunking & Contextual Retrieval
lessons.goal: Understand how documents are split into chunks, how context is added, and why embedding quality caps retrieval recall.

cards.title: Chunking and Context Segmentation
cards.text: Chunking splits external data into contiguous text segments that are embedded and retrieved independently, so the chunk becomes the atomic unit of knowledge in RAG. Small chunks match queries precisely and raise recall but lose surrounding context; large chunks keep coherence but lower recall and drag in irrelevant text. Typical sizes are 200-500 tokens, often with overlap so information at boundaries is not cut apart, at the cost of extra storage and compute. Better strategies align chunks with semantic units such as sentences or document sections.
points: Chunk = contiguous text segment, embedded and retrieved independently
Recall = fraction of relevant chunks that appear in the retrieved results
Small chunks: higher recall, precise matching, less context
Large chunks: more coherence, lower recall, more irrelevant info
Typical size 200-500 tokens, often with overlap
Advanced: sentence-based, semantic, section-aware chunking; bad chunking cannot be fixed downstream
cards.formula: Consecutive chunks: chunk size L and overlap O share O tokens, so stride = L - O; Recall = |relevant intersect retrieved| / |relevant|
cards.example: With L = 400 and O = 100, each 400-token chunk overlaps the next by 100 tokens, so a sentence split on a boundary still appears whole in one of them.
cards.say: Documents are too big to feed whole, so we cut them into chunks and treat each chunk as one searchable unit. Overlap keeps a sentence that straddles two chunks from being lost, but it costs extra storage and work.

scene.text: Refunds take 5 days. Bring your receipt. Gift cards are final. Ask at the desk.

items.tip: Chunk 1. Each chunk is embedded and retrieved on its own: the atomic unit of knowledge.
Chunk 2. Small chunks match questions precisely and raise recall, but lose surrounding context.
Chunk 3. Large chunks keep coherence but lower recall and drag in irrelevant text.
Recall = relevant chunks retrieved divided by all relevant chunks.

beats.cap: You cannot hand a model a whole library, so you cut the text into bite-sized pieces called chunks.
Each chunk is embedded and searched on its own, so a chunk is the smallest unit the system can find.
Tiny chunks match questions sharply but lose context, while huge chunks keep the story but bury the answer in noise.
A common size is two hundred to five hundred tokens, say four hundred, with the next one overlapping by one hundred.
Cutting along sentences or sections works best, because a bad cut can never be repaired later in the pipeline.

cards.title: Contextual Retrieval
cards.text: A chunk on its own may lack the information needed to understand it, for example a sentence saying revenue grew by 3% without naming the company or the period. Contextual retrieval fixes this by giving an LLM the full document and asking it to write a short context description for each chunk. That description is prepended to the chunk before embedding, so each chunk becomes self-contained and its embedding captures both local content and document-level meaning.
points: A chunk can be ambiguous because it lacks document-level context
An LLM reads the full document and writes a short context per chunk
The context is prepended to the chunk text
The enriched text is embedded
Chunks become self-contained; embeddings encode local plus global meaning
cards.example: Original chunk: 'The company's revenue grew by 3% over the previous quarter.' Contextualized: 'This chunk is from an SEC filing on ACME corp's performance in Q2 2023; the previous quarter's revenue was $314 million. The company's revenue grew by 3% over the previous quarter.'
cards.say: A chunk like revenue grew by three percent is useless on its own because we do not know whose revenue. Contextual retrieval has a model read the whole document and write a short lead-in for each chunk, so the chunk explains itself before it is embedded.

items.l: Chunk: The company's revenue grew by 3% over the previous quarter.
items.tip: Ambiguous on its own: which company, which quarter?

items.l: Here is the full document. Write a short context for this chunk.
items.tip: An LLM reads the whole document once for each chunk.

items.l: From ACME corp's SEC filing for Q2 2023; previous quarter revenue was $314 million.
items.tip: A short description of where the chunk sits in the document.
The context is prepended, then the enriched text is embedded.

beats.cap: Imagine finding a torn page that says revenue grew three percent. Whose revenue? Which quarter? No idea.
Contextual retrieval asks a language model to read the whole document and describe where this chunk belongs.
It writes that the chunk comes from an ACME filing for the second quarter of 2023.
That note is glued to the front of the chunk before embedding, so the chunk now explains itself.

cards.title: Embedding Quality and Retrieval Recall
cards.text: Embedding quality sets the ceiling for how much relevant information a RAG system can ever retrieve. A relevant chunk is found only if it is more similar to the query than the irrelevant chunks; if the geometry does not put it close, no later stage can bring it back. Recall is driven mainly by the embedding model, its domain alignment, the chunking strategy, how the query is phrased and the nearest-neighbor search. Rerankers and LLMs only reorder or use what was retrieved, so they cannot fix missing recall.
points: Embedding quality determines the maximum achievable recall
Chunks not close to the query are never retrieved
Retrieval failure is a representation problem
Recall drivers: model choice, domain alignment, chunking, query formulation, NN search
Rerankers and LLMs cannot fix missing recall
Failure chain: weak embeddings -> missing evidence -> parametric guess -> hallucination
cards.formula: Retrieval succeeds only if cos_sim(q, d_relevant) > cos_sim(q, d_irrelevant)
cards.example: Lower the embedding quality until the relevant chunk falls below the top-k cut-off: no reranker can recover it, because it never entered the candidate list.
cards.say: The embedding model decides how much you can ever find. If the right chunk does not land near the question in vector space, nothing later in the pipeline can rescue it, and the model falls back on its own memory.
covers: A9: Embedding Quality and Retrieval Recall

items.tip: Weak embeddings placed this irrelevant chunk closer to the query.
Also irrelevant, but inside the top 2.
Relevant, yet below the top-k cut-off. It never enters the candidate list.
Correctly far away.

beats.cap: Think of a fishing net: whatever never gets caught can never be cooked, no matter how good the chef is.
A chunk is retrieved only if it scores closer to the query than the irrelevant chunks around it.
Here weak embeddings let two off-topic chunks win the top two spots, and the right chunk misses the cut.
A reranker or the model only works with what was caught, so the missing evidence becomes a guess, then a hallucination.
Recall depends on the embedding model, domain fit, chunking, query wording and the search itself.

lessons.title: Vector Stores & ANN Search
lessons.goal: See why exact search is too slow at scale and how vector stores use approximate indexes, clustering and quantization.

cards.title: Naive Search vs. Vector Stores
cards.text: After embedding, the system must find the stored vectors most similar to the query. Doing this naively means computing similarity with every stored vector, which costs O(N) per query and is far too slow when there are millions or billions of chunks with hundreds or thousands of dimensions and a millisecond latency budget. A vector store (vector database) stores embeddings and retrieves them by similarity instead of exact keys, typically offering approximate nearest-neighbor search and metadata filtering by source, date or access rights.
points: Naive search compares q against all stored vectors: O(N) per query
Infeasible at millions to billions of chunks with millisecond latency
Vector store = storage plus retrieval of embeddings by similarity
Provides high-dimensional storage, ANN search and metadata filtering
Core idea: trade exactness for speed while preserving high recall
cards.formula: Exact search: argmax_i cos_sim(q, d_i), cost O(N) per query (N = number of stored vectors)
cards.example: With a billion chunks of hundreds of dimensions, a scan per query is hopeless against a millisecond budget, so the index must inspect only a small subset of vectors.
cards.say: The obvious way to find the closest stored vector is to compare the query with every single one, but that becomes far too slow once you have millions of chunks. A vector store keeps the same idea but adds an index so only a small part is ever examined.
covers: A9: Naive Search vs. Vector Stores

items.tip: Compare the query with every stored vector: cost grows with N, for every single query.
Illustrative: an approximate index inspects only a small subset of the vectors.

beats.cap: Finding a book by reading every page in the library would work, but you would be there forever.
Naive search compares your query with every stored vector. With a billion chunks, that misses a millisecond budget badly.
A vector store keeps embeddings and finds them by similarity, peeking at only a small subset of them.
It also filters by source, date or access rights, and trades a little exactness for huge speed.

cards.title: Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
cards.text: ANN search aims to find vectors that are close enough to the true nearest neighbors much faster than scanning everything. It works by organizing vectors into a structured index and inspecting only a small subset, reducing latency and memory traffic. In RAG this approximation is acceptable because several relevant chunks usually exist and small similarity differences rarely change answer quality, so coverage (recall) matters more than perfect ordering. The index parameters let engineers tune between fast-but-lossy and slower-but-higher-recall retrieval.
points: Goal: near-nearest neighbors, much faster than a full scan
Uses a structured index and searches only a small subset
In RAG, high recall matters more than exact ordering
The vector index determines speed, memory and recall
Recall versus latency is tunable through index parameters
ANN is the first-stage candidate retrieval that produces top-k
cards.example: An 'effort' slider on the index traces a recall-versus-latency curve: more effort visits more points for higher recall at higher latency.
cards.say: Instead of checking every vector, an approximate index checks only a promising subset. It may miss the exact best match, but for retrieval that is fine as long as the right answers stay near the top. One knob trades latency against recall.

items.tip: Visits few points: very quick, but some true neighbors are missed.
Most relevant chunks found at low latency. Typical RAG setting.
Visits many points: close to exact search, but costly.

beats.cap: You do not need the single best restaurant in town, just a few great ones nearby, and fast.
Approximate search uses a structured index and checks only a small part of it, so it finds near neighbors quickly.
In retrieval this is fine, because several chunks are usually relevant and tiny score differences rarely change the answer.
Turn up the effort and the index visits more points, recall rises, but so does waiting time. Drag to explore.

cards.title: Inverted File Index (IVF)
cards.text: IVF speeds up search by clustering. During training, k centroids are learned with k-means and every vector is assigned to its nearest centroid. At query time the system first finds the centroids closest to the query and then searches only the vectors inside those clusters. This is much faster than a flat scan and scales to large datasets, but recall depends on how many clusters are probed: a true neighbor sitting in an unsearched cluster is missed.
points: Search within clusters instead of all vectors
Training: k-means learns k centroids; each vector is assigned to its nearest centroid
Query time: find nearest centroids, search only their clusters
Much faster than flat search and scales well
Recall depends on the number of clusters probed
Can miss neighbors in unprobed clusters, e.g. near a boundary
cards.example: A query lands in one Voronoi cell; if the right neighbor sits just across a boundary in an unprobed cell, IVF never looks at it and the match is lost.
cards.say: IVF groups the vectors into clusters ahead of time. A query only looks inside the few clusters nearest to it instead of everywhere, which is far faster, but a true neighbour could hide in a cluster you never opened.

items.tip: Learned by k-means during training. Each vector belongs to its nearest centroid.
Another cluster center. Its cluster is a Voronoi cell.
Third cluster center.
Closest to centroid A, so only cluster A is searched.
The best match inside the probed cluster.
Just across the boundary in cluster B, which was not probed. Probing more clusters helps.

beats.cap: Think of a supermarket: to find pasta, you walk straight to the right aisle instead of checking every shelf.
During training, k-means picks cluster centers, and every vector joins the center closest to it.
A query first finds its nearest center, then searches only inside that cluster. Much faster, and it scales.
But the true nearest neighbor sits just across the border in an aisle nobody checked, so it is lost.

cards.title: Quantization-Based Indexes
cards.text: Quantization reduces the memory footprint of vectors by compressing them, storing fewer bits per dimension and approximating each vector via codebooks. Distances are then computed approximately on the compressed codes, which cuts memory bandwidth and speeds up access. Product quantization and scalar quantization are the typical examples. This enables retrieval over very large collections, at the cost of lower precision and a slight loss of recall.
points: Compress vectors: fewer bits stored per dimension
Vectors are approximated using codebooks
Distances are computed approximately on the codes
Examples: product quantization, scalar quantization
Pros: much lower memory, faster memory access, very large scale
Cons: lower precision and a slight recall degradation
cards.example: A full-precision vector snaps to the nearest codebook levels, like pixelation: the memory meter drops sharply while a small similarity error appears.
cards.say: Quantization shrinks each vector by storing fewer bits per number. That saves a lot of memory and speeds up the distance calculation, at the price of a little precision, which is usually acceptable for retrieval.

items.tip: Example: 768 dimensions with 32-bit floats, 4 bytes each.
Each number snaps to one of 256 levels: one byte per dimension.
Example: split into 96 pieces, store one codebook ID byte per piece.

beats.cap: Quantization is like pixelating a photo: it gets a little blurry, but the file shrinks dramatically.
Instead of full precision numbers, each vector stores fewer bits, snapping values to the nearest codebook entry.
Product quantization goes further, and distances are computed straight from these compact codes.
Memory drops sharply and lookups speed up, letting you search huge collections, at the cost of slightly lower recall.

cards.title: FAISS and Index Comparison
cards.text: FAISS (Facebook AI Similarity Search) is Meta's open-source library for fast similarity search and clustering of dense vectors, with CPU and GPU implementations. It focuses on algorithms and performance rather than database features and is a baseline in research and industry. It implements most major index types: Flat (exact), IVF, HNSW, Product Quantization, and IVF-PQ which combines IVF routing with PQ compression. Comparing indexes is a systems-engineering decision about the speed-accuracy trade-off, not a modeling choice.
points: FAISS: Meta/FAIR, open source, CPU and GPU
Focus on algorithms and performance, not database features
Implements Flat, IVF, HNSW, PQ and IVF-PQ
Flat: high memory, high recall, low speed
IVF: medium memory, recall and speed
HNSW: high memory, high recall, high speed; Quantized: low memory, medium recall, very high speed
cards.example: Comparison table (memory/recall/speed): Flat high/high/low; IVF medium/medium/medium; HNSW high/high/high; Quantized low/medium/very high.
cards.say: FAISS is a widely used open-source library that offers all the main index types, from exact flat search to IVF, graph-based HNSW and quantized indexes. Picking one is really about the trade-off between memory, recall and speed for your data size.

items.tip: Facebook AI Similarity Search: Meta's open-source library, CPU and GPU. Algorithms, not database features.
Exact search. Memory high, recall high, speed low.
Cluster routing. Memory medium, recall medium, speed medium.
Layered graph. Memory high, recall high, speed high.
Quantized. Memory low, recall medium, speed very high.
IVF routing to clusters plus PQ compression inside them.

beats.cap: FAISS is like a toolbox of search engines, open source from Meta, running on ordinary processors or graphics cards.
It focuses on fast algorithms rather than database features, and it is a standard baseline everywhere.
Flat is exact but slow, IVF is middle of the road, and HNSW is fast with high recall but memory hungry.
Quantized indexes are tiny and very fast with medium recall, and IVF-PQ combines routing with compression.
Choosing between them is an engineering trade-off of speed, memory and accuracy, not a modeling choice.

lessons.title: Graph Search: NSW & HNSW
lessons.goal: Understand how navigable small world graphs are built and searched, and how skip-list layering gives HNSW its speed.

cards.title: NSW Graphs: Building
cards.text: Navigable Small World (NSW) graphs borrow the idea of six degrees of separation: each embedding is a node connected to a few highly similar nodes, so any node can be reached in few hops, and the number of edges per node is kept small. The graph is built by inserting nodes one at a time. For a new node, a greedy search starts from an entry node and keeps moving to whichever neighbor is more similar until no closer node exists. Then connections are chosen under three constraints: at most M neighbors, prefer closer nodes, and reject a candidate very close to an already chosen neighbor to keep links diverse.
points: Inspired by six degrees of separation
Nodes are embeddings; edges connect similar nodes, kept few per node
Insertion: greedy search from the entry point, moving to a closer neighbor until no improvement
Constraint 1: maximum degree M
Constraint 2: prefer closer nodes
Constraint 3: diversity - reject a candidate very close to an already chosen neighbor
cards.example: Insert e6 with M = 2: from e1 (cos_sim 0.1) move to e4 (0.7); connect e6 to e4. Candidate e5 (0.4) is rejected because it is very close to e4 (0.8), so e6 connects to e3 (0.2) instead; the graph gains edges e6-e4 and e6-e3.
cards.say: A navigable small world graph links each vector to a handful of similar ones so any point can be reached in a few steps. To insert a new point we hop greedily toward its closest matches, then keep only a few edges, preferring close neighbors but also keeping them varied.
covers: A9: Navigable Small World Graphs: Building

items.tip: Greedy search ends here: no neighbor of e4 is closer to e6. First link: e6 to e4.
Rejected for diversity: e5 is very close to e4, similarity 0.8, so it adds little.
Second link: further away, but points in a different direction.
Entry point where the greedy search started.

beats.cap: Remember six degrees of separation? Anyone can reach anyone through a few friends. These graphs copy that idea.
Each embedding is a node with only a few links to similar nodes. New nodes are added one at a time.
To add e6, start at e1 and keep hopping to a more similar neighbor, reaching e4 at zero point seven.
With at most two links, e5 looks good but sits right next to e4, so e3 is chosen instead.
Three rules: a maximum of M links, prefer closer nodes, and keep the links diverse.

cards.title: NSW Graphs: Searching
cards.text: To search, the algorithm picks a random entry node, computes the query's similarity to that node and its neighbors, records the scores, and moves to the neighbor with the highest similarity. This repeats until it reaches a node whose neighbors are all less similar, a local best. The k nodes with the highest recorded similarity scores are returned as the result. Because only a path of nodes is evaluated, search is far cheaper than scanning all vectors, though greedy search can stop at a local optimum.
points: Start at a random entry point
Compare the query to the entry and its neighbors
Store the scores of all evaluated nodes
Move to the node with the highest similarity
Stop at a local-best node
Return the top-k nodes among the evaluated scores
cards.example: Query q enters at e3 (cos_sim 0.1); its neighbors are e2 (0.4) and e6 (0.7), so move to e6. No neighbor beats 0.7, so e6 is the local best; with k = 2 the result is e6 (0.7) and e2 (0.4).
cards.say: Searching walks along the graph from a random start toward nodes that look more and more similar. It stops when no neighbour is closer, then returns the best few points it recorded along the way. It is fast, but it can get stuck at a merely local best.
covers: A9: Navigable Small World Graphs: Searching

items.tip: Random entry point. Its score is computed and recorded.
Neighbor of e3, recorded.
Best neighbor, so move here. None of its neighbors beat 0.7: a local best.

beats.cap: Searching is like asking for directions: each person points you to someone who knows a bit more.
The query enters at a random node, e3, scoring only zero point one, then checks its neighbors.
Neighbor e6 scores zero point seven, the best, so we hop there. Nothing around it does better, so we stop.
From all the scores we wrote down, the top two are returned: e6 and e2.
Only nodes along the path were checked, far cheaper than a full scan, though greedy hops can stop at a local best.

cards.title: Skip Lists
cards.text: A skip list is a probabilistic data structure with several stacked linked lists: the bottom level holds all elements, and each higher level holds fewer, which lets a search skip over many items at once. Searching starts at the top level, moves along to the locally best element, then drops down a level and refines. In the example the similarity is alphabet distance and the target is C: at the top the search reaches B, descends, finds C closer to B than E, descends again, finds B and D equally close, descends, and finally moves right to reach C at the bottom level.
points: Multiple linked-list levels; higher levels are sparser
Fast traversal by skipping over many items
Per level: find the local best, then move down a level
Search from the top down to the full bottom level
Inspiration for the layered structure of HNSW
cards.example: Levels L3 {B}, L2 {B, E}, L1 {B, D, E}, L0 {A, B, C, D, E, F}: searching for C with alphabet distance reaches B at L3, descends through L2 and L1, then moves right from B to C at L0.
cards.say: A skip list stacks several sorted lists so that the top ones are sparse and let you jump far. You move right as far as you can, drop down a level to refine, and repeat, which is a fast way to find one item among many.

items.tip: Top level holds only B. Similarity here is distance in the alphabet, target is C.
Level 2 holds B and E. C is closer to B than to E, so stay at B and drop.
Level 1 holds B, D and E. B and D are equally close to C, so drop again.
Bottom level holds all of A to F. Move right from B and arrive at C.

beats.cap: Think of express and local trains: you ride the express to get close, then switch to the local train.
A skip list stacks linked lists. The bottom one holds everything, each higher level holds fewer items.
Looking for C, we reach B at the top, then drop down because C sits closer to B than E.
At the full bottom level we take one step right and land on C. This layering inspires HNSW.

cards.title: Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW)
cards.text: HNSW combines NSW graphs with the skip-list idea by building multiple graph layers: upper layers contain few nodes with long-range links, and the bottom layer contains all nodes. A search begins at an entry point on the highest layer, greedily moves toward the query, then descends layer by layer and refines in the denser graphs. This gives an excellent speed-recall trade-off with high recall at low latency, which is why HNSW is widely used in production and is the typical default for RAG.
points: HNSW = NSW graph plus skip-list layering
Multi-layer graph: sparse upper layers and a full bottom layer
Search starts at the highest layer from an entry point, then descends
Excellent speed-recall trade-off: high recall at low latency
Widely used in production; the typical default for RAG
cards.example: Layer L1 contains e1 and e4 while layer L0 contains e1-e5: the search starts at L1, hops greedily, then drops to L0 to refine among all nodes.
cards.say: HNSW stacks these small-world graphs into layers, just like a skip list. Search hops quickly through the sparse top layers and then drops down to refine in the dense bottom one, giving high recall with very low latency, which is why it is the usual default.

items.tip: Bottom layer contains every node: the full, dense graph for fine search.
Sparse upper layer with long-range links for big jumps.
Search always begins at the entry point on the highest layer.

beats.cap: Now combine both ideas: a small-world graph, stacked in layers like the express trains of a skip list.
Upper layers hold few nodes with long jumps, while the bottom layer holds every single node.
The search starts at the top entry point, hops greedily toward the query, then drops down and refines.
That gives high recall at low latency, which is why HNSW is the usual default for retrieval.

lessons.title: Retrieval: Dense, Sparse, Hybrid
lessons.goal: Compare dense and sparse retrieval, see why they are combined, and learn how Reciprocal Rank Fusion merges their rankings.

cards.title: Dense Retrieval
cards.text: Dense retrieval embeds queries and chunks into the same vector space and returns the top-k chunks by cosine similarity, so it matches meaning rather than exact words. It is the default first stage in most RAG pipelines, tuned for high recall, and it supplies candidates to a reranker. It excels at paraphrases, synonyms, conceptual similarity and natural-language questions. It struggles with rare identifiers such as IDs or serial numbers, exact string matches, numeric constraints and rare proper names.
points: Retrieves by semantic similarity in a shared vector space
Default first stage, optimized for high recall
Produces candidates for reranking
Strong on paraphrases, synonyms, concepts and natural questions
Weak on rare IDs, exact strings, numeric constraints and rare proper names
cards.formula: Top-k = argmax_i cos_sim(q, d_i): the k chunks with the highest cosine similarity to the query embedding q
cards.example: 'How do transformers handle long-range dependencies?' retrieves relevant documents even without exact word overlap, because the meaning is captured by the vectors.
cards.say: Dense retrieval searches by meaning. It turns the question and the chunks into vectors and returns the closest ones, so it finds paraphrases well. But it can miss a rare serial number or an exact phrase where the wording really matters.

items.tip: Same meaning in different words lands nearby in vector space.
Car and automobile point the same way.
How do transformers handle long-range dependencies finds good docs without exact word overlap.
Everyday phrasing works because meaning, not wording, is matched.
An ID like XK-4471 carries little meaning for an embedding.
Similar meaning is not the same as the exact text you need.
Under 50 euros and over 50 euros look almost identical as vectors.
Uncommon proper names are poorly represented.

beats.cap: Dense retrieval is like a librarian who understands what you mean, even when you use different words.
Query and chunks share one vector space, and the top k chunks by cosine similarity come back.
Asking how transformers handle long-range dependencies finds good documents, even without matching words.
But it stumbles on rare IDs, exact strings, number limits and unusual names.
It is the usual first stage, tuned to catch as much as possible, then handing candidates to a reranker.

cards.title: Sparse Retrieval (BM25)
cards.text: Sparse retrieval represents text by explicit word occurrences, with one dimension per vocabulary word and mostly zeros, and scores documents by exact word overlap. BM25 (Best Matching 25, from the Okapi IR system; the number is historical) is the standard rule-based, non-learned ranking function. It rewards documents containing the query terms, especially rare terms (high IDF), counts repeated occurrences with diminishing returns (saturation), and normalizes for document length so long documents are not unfairly favored.
points: Sparse vector: one dimension per vocabulary word, mostly zeros
BM25 is rule-based, not learned; it comes from the Okapi system
IDF: rare query words weigh more than common ones
Term frequency saturates: the first occurrences help most
Length normalization treats short and long documents fairly
Strong for exact keywords, IDs, proper names and legal or technical references, but cannot match paraphrases
cards.formula: score(q, d) = sum over terms t in q of IDF(t) * TF(t, d) / (TF(t, d) + normalization(d)); TF = occurrences of t in d, IDF = rarity of t in the corpus, normalization(d) = length-dependent term
cards.example: Query 'EU AI Act Article 52' is split into terms {EU, AI, Act, Article, 52}. Common words like 'the' have low IDF while a rare word like 'RoPE' has high IDF, so matching it counts far more.
cards.say: Sparse retrieval is old-school keyword matching done well. BM25 gives extra weight to rare query words, counts repeats with diminishing returns, and normalizes for document length, so it nails exact terms like article numbers but cannot understand paraphrases.

items.tip: Fairly common term: moderate IDF.
Very common in a tech corpus: low IDF, small weight.
A legal keyword, exact match matters.
Common in legal text: lower weight.
Rare and precise: high IDF. Repeats help with diminishing returns, and long docs are normalized.

beats.cap: Sparse retrieval is like a book index: it simply looks for the exact words you typed.
Your query is split into terms, and each document gets a long list with one slot per word, mostly zeros.
BM25 scores by overlap, and rare words count more: matching fifty two is worth far more than matching the word the.
Repeating a word helps less each time, and long documents get no unfair advantage.
It needs no training and nails IDs, names and legal references, but it cannot match paraphrases.

cards.title: Hybrid Retrieval
cards.text: Dense and sparse retrieval have complementary strengths: dense captures meaning, while BM25 captures exact keywords. Hybrid retrieval runs both, obtaining semantic and lexical candidate lists, fuses the ranked lists, and passes the merged candidates on to reranking or generation. This increases robustness and recall. A popular fusion method is Reciprocal Rank Fusion, which ignores raw scores and uses only rank positions, rewarding documents ranked highly in any list and especially those ranked well in several lists.
points: Dense gives semantic similarity; sparse gives exact keyword matching
Hybrid combines both for robustness and recall
Pipeline: run dense, run BM25, fuse rankings, then rerank or generate
Fusion uses rank positions rather than raw scores
Documents high in multiple lists are strongly rewarded
cards.example: A conceptual question is answered well by the dense list while an exact article number is found by the BM25 list; merging the two recovers both kinds of relevant chunk.
cards.say: Dense and keyword search fail in opposite ways, so we simply run both. The meaning-based list and the exact-word list are then merged, and the combined ranking is more robust than either one alone.

items.tip: For example a conceptual question that also mentions an exact article number.
Semantic candidate list: finds chunks with the right meaning.
Lexical candidate list: finds the chunk with the exact article number.
Uses rank positions, not raw scores. Chunks high in several lists are strongly rewarded.
The merged candidates move on, with better robustness and recall.

beats.cap: Why choose between a librarian who understands meaning and an index that finds exact words? Use both.
Run dense search for meaning and BM25 for exact keywords, getting two candidate lists side by side.
The lists are merged by rank position, so chunks that rank well in both lists rise to the top.
The conceptual answer and the exact article are both recovered, then passed to reranking or the model.

cards.title: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
cards.text: RRF scores each document by summing 1/(k + rank) over every retrieval system that returned it. Higher ranks give larger contributions, lower ranks contribute rapidly less, and appearing in multiple lists accumulates score, so a document ranked first and second beats one ranked first in only one list. It is scale-invariant (no score normalization needed), robust to noisy rankings, works across very different retrievers and has a single hyperparameter k, typically about 60.
points: Score = sum of reciprocal ranks over the retrieval systems
k of about 60 smooths the differences between ranks
Scale-invariant: no score normalization needed
Robust to noisy rankings and heterogeneous retrievers
Only one hyperparameter (k)
Consistency across lists beats a single top rank
cards.formula: RRF(d) = sum over systems i of 1 / (k + rank_i(d)), where rank_i(d) is the rank of document d in system i and k is a smoothing constant, typically about 60
cards.example: Dense ranking: 1 chunk2, 2 chunk1, 3 chunk3; BM25 ranking: 1 chunk1, 2 chunk4, 3 chunk2. RRF(chunk1) = 1/(60+2) + 1/(60+1) = 123/3782 = 0.03252, RRF(chunk2) = 1/(60+1) + 1/(60+3) = 124/3843 = 0.03227, so chunk1 narrowly wins despite never ranking first everywhere.
cards.say: Reciprocal rank fusion ignores the actual scores and looks only at positions. Each list adds one over k plus the rank, so a document that appears near the top of several lists wins overall, even if it never comes first in any single one.

items.tip: Dense rank 2, BM25 rank 1: 1 over 62 plus 1 over 61 = 0.03252.
Dense rank 1, BM25 rank 3: 1 over 61 plus 1 over 63 = 0.03227.
Only BM25 rank 2: 1 over 62.
Only dense rank 3: 1 over 63.

beats.cap: Imagine two judges ranking dancers. Instead of comparing their score sheets, you only look at the places they gave.
Each list gives a document one over sixty plus its rank, and you add up the gifts.
Chunk two was first in dense but third in BM25. Chunk one was second and first.
Chunk one narrowly wins, while chunks seen in only one list fall far behind.
No score scaling needed, it tolerates noisy rankings, and its only setting is k, usually around sixty.

quiz.q: What does the 'P' in ChatGPT stand for?
quiz.answer: Pretrained
quiz.why: GPT means Generative Pretrained Transformer: the model first learns broad knowledge from large text corpora.

quiz.q: Which of these did NOT contribute to ChatGPT's rapid adoption?
quiz.answer: Users had to write code to interact with it
distractors: A free tier lowered the entry barrier
It remembered the conversation within a session
Impressive answers were shared virally on social media
quiz.why: A central success factor was that no technical expertise was needed at all.

quiz.q: What is the key shift from traditional machine learning to generative AI?
quiz.answer: From one specialised model per task to one model handling many tasks
distractors: From neural networks to rule-based systems
From one task per model to many models per task
quiz.why: Classic ML trained a separate model for each task; a foundation model is general-purpose.

quiz.q: Which Transformer property is named as a driver of generative AI?
quiz.answer: Self-attention that can be trained in a highly parallel way
distractors: Processing one token at a time recurrently
quiz.why: Parallel self-attention made training on web-scale data with GPU clusters practical.

quiz.q: What is the main downside of the AI race described in this lesson?
quiz.answer: Pressure to release products before they are mature
distractors: Lower energy demand from data centres
quiz.why: Competition speeds progress but pushes companies to ship early.

quiz.q: For 'The cat sits on the' with mat 0.70, sofa 0.15, chair 0.10, car 0.05, what does greedy (argmax) selection output?
quiz.answer: mat
distractors: A random word weighted by probability
quiz.why: Argmax picks the single most probable candidate, which is 'mat' at 0.70.

quiz.q: What is autoregressive generation?
quiz.answer: Repeatedly predicting, selecting and appending one token at a time
distractors: Generating the whole answer in one parallel step
Regressing a continuous number from text
quiz.why: Each chosen token is appended to the input and the model predicts again.

quiz.q: Why is language model training called self-supervised?
quiz.answer: The labels (next words) come directly from the raw text
distractors: Humans label every word by hand
The model trains without any data
It uses reinforcement learning from human feedback
quiz.why: Each next word in the text serves as the target, so no manual annotation is needed.

quiz.q: A bigram model has a vocabulary of 50,000 words. Roughly how many entries does its probability table need?
quiz.answer: 2.5 billion
quiz.why: A bigram table has V^2 entries: 50,000^2 = 2.5 x 10^9. (125 trillion would be a trigram, V^3.)

quiz.q: In speech recognition, why is 'I eat ice cream' chosen over 'I eat I scream'?
quiz.answer: The language model assigns the first sentence a higher probability
distractors: The audio signals are clearly different
quiz.why: Both sound identical; the LM re-ranks acoustic hypotheses by linguistic plausibility.

quiz.q: Beyond next-token prediction, which three aspects explain a model's capabilities?
quiz.answer: Architecture; training and alignment; inference and context
quiz.why: Prediction is only the generation mechanism; capability comes from how the model is built, trained and prompted.

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of the three scaling dimensions of LLMs?
quiz.answer: Number of human annotators
quiz.why: LLMs scale data, parameters and compute; being self-supervised, they do not depend on annotators.

quiz.q: An LLM trained only on next-token prediction can also translate and write code. What are such skills called?
quiz.answer: Emergent abilities
quiz.why: They emerge at scale from the prediction objective without explicit task training.

quiz.q: Why was 'foundation model' preferred over 'general-purpose model'?
quiz.answer: It conveys that the model is an unfinished base that needs adaptation
distractors: It refers only to text models
It describes the self-supervised learning method
It means the model never needs prompting or fine-tuning
quiz.why: 'General-purpose' signals versatility but hides that the model must be adapted to downstream tasks.

quiz.q: Which statement correctly relates LLMs, foundation models and AI systems?
quiz.answer: An LLM is a type of foundation model; an AI system combines models with context, data, tools and logic
distractors: A foundation model is a type of LLM
An AI system is just another name for an LLM
LLMs are trained only on images
quiz.why: LLMs are the text specialisation of foundation models; AI systems wrap models into usable applications.

quiz.q: Which statement about ChatGPT is correct?
quiz.answer: It uses a foundation model but is not itself a foundation model
distractors: It is a raw foundation model with no extra layers
It has used GPT-4 since its 2022 launch
quiz.why: ChatGPT = foundation model + alignment + interface, and it launched on GPT-3.5.

quiz.q: Which model is the example of an audio/speech foundation model?
quiz.answer: Whisper
quiz.why: Whisper learns from raw and transcribed speech; CLIP is vision, Sora is video, DALL-E generates images.

quiz.q: AI engineering is best described as the discipline of...
quiz.answer: building reliable, useful and maintainable systems around AI models
distractors: training foundation models from scratch only
quiz.why: It centres on building applications with foundation models as core components.

quiz.q: In the AI engineering stack, which concerns cut across all layers?
quiz.answer: Evaluation, safety and monitoring
quiz.why: Testing, red teaming, guardrails, monitoring and feedback loops apply to every layer.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT one of the six core capabilities?
quiz.answer: Blockchain
quiz.why: The six are vision, language, audio, code, tool use and reasoning.

quiz.q: What is the typical loop of a coding assistant?
quiz.answer: Generate code -> run tests -> inspect results -> refine
quiz.why: Coding assistants iterate using execution and testing tools; search-compare-decide-act is the agent pattern.

quiz.q: A demo asks 'Can the model do this?'. What does a production AI system ask?
quiz.answer: Can the system do this reliably, safely and efficiently?
distractors: Can the model produce one impressive answer?
Is this the largest model available?
quiz.why: Production requires consistent behaviour across many cases plus safety, latency and cost control.

quiz.q: The model invents a contract clause that sounds plausible but does not exist. Which failure category is this?
quiz.answer: Factuality
quiz.why: Plausible but incorrect content is a factuality failure, often called hallucination.

quiz.q: Why does 'open-weight' not mean 'open-source'?
quiz.answer: Published weights do not imply that training code, data or the full process are public
distractors: Open-weight models cannot be run locally
Open-weight models come without any license
quiz.why: Only the trained parameters are released, under a license; other artefacts may stay closed.

quiz.q: What is the role of llama.cpp within Ollama?
quiz.answer: It is the open-source inference library Ollama uses to run LLMs locally
distractors: It is a cloud API for GPT-4
It is a drag-and-drop workflow editor
It is a dataset of open-weight models
quiz.why: Ollama builds on llama.cpp and adds model downloading plus CLI, GUI and HTTP access.

quiz.q: Approximately how much weight memory does an 8B-parameter model need at 4-bit precision?
quiz.answer: About 4 GB
quiz.why: 8e9 parameters x 4 bits / 8 = 4e9 bytes, about 4 GB.

quiz.q: What is the engineering lesson of the 'find a model that fits your hardware' challenge?
quiz.answer: Model selection is a trade-off between quality, memory and speed
distractors: Always choose the largest model that fits
Speed does not matter for local models
quiz.why: A smaller or quantised model may be nearly as good while far faster and lighter.

quiz.q: What is LangFlow?
quiz.answer: A visual GUI for building LangChain workflows by connecting blocks
distractors: A local LLM runtime based on llama.cpp
quiz.why: LangFlow is the drag-and-drop front end for LangChain and can export Python code.

quiz.q: What does 'vibe coding' describe?
quiz.answer: Building software mainly by describing it to an AI and accepting its code with little review
distractors: Pair programming with a human colleague
quiz.why: The term, coined in early 2025, refers to programming through natural-language instructions to an AI.

quiz.q: In the newer course roadmap, which part contains retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)?
quiz.answer: Build with Models
quiz.why: Part 2, Build with Models, holds prompt engineering, agents, RAG and fine-tuning.

quiz.q: What is required to pass each graded computer lab unit?
quiz.answer: At least 50% of the points
quiz.why: Every graded unit requires at least half of the points; Unit 0 is optional.

quiz.q: What does BOF4 stand for?
quiz.answer: 4-bit Block-Wise Optimal Float
quiz.why: BOF4 is a 4-bit block-wise quantisation format for LLM weights, published at ICLR 2026.

quiz.q: Which tool is used in the lab for RAG?
quiz.answer: ChromaDB
quiz.why: The lab's RAG unit uses the ChromaDB vector database.

quiz.q: Which order correctly describes the text-to-text pipeline?
quiz.answer: Tokenization -> embedding lookup -> forward pass -> token selection -> detokenization
distractors: Embedding lookup -> tokenization -> forward pass -> detokenization -> token selection
Detokenization -> tokenization -> forward pass -> embedding lookup -> token selection
Tokenization -> forward pass -> embedding lookup -> token selection -> detokenization
quiz.why: Text becomes IDs, IDs become vectors, the model scores every token, one is chosen, and it is decoded back to text.

quiz.q: What does the LLM itself output right before a token is chosen?
quiz.answer: Logits: one raw score for every vocabulary token
distractors: The next word as a string
An embedding vector for the next word
A single token ID decided internally
quiz.why: The forward pass only scores candidates; a separate selection step makes the choice.

quiz.q: How many new tokens does one forward pass of a causal LLM produce during generation?
quiz.answer: Exactly one
distractors: One per word in the prompt
As many as fit in the context window
quiz.why: Generation is autoregressive: each pass scores only the next token, which is appended before the next pass.

quiz.q: Why does the pipeline need an embedding lookup after tokenization?
quiz.answer: Token IDs are arbitrary indices; the network needs meaningful continuous vectors
distractors: IDs are too long to store in memory
The tokenizer outputs letters, not numbers
Embeddings compress the text to save API cost
quiz.why: An ID is just a catalogue number; the learned vector is what the network computes with.

quiz.q: In the BPE example on the corpus 'low lower', which pair is merged first?
quiz.answer: (l, o)
quiz.why: (l, o) is the most frequent adjacent pair, so it becomes the new token 'lo'.

quiz.q: Why does byte-level BPE never encounter an unknown input character?
quiz.answer: Its base vocabulary holds all 256 byte values, and every UTF-8 character is 1-4 bytes
distractors: It contains a dictionary of all words in all languages
It maps unknown characters to the padding token
It retrains the tokenizer at inference time
quiz.why: Any text is a byte sequence, and each byte is already a token.

quiz.q: What is a main drawback of a word-level vocabulary?
quiz.answer: A huge vocabulary and no way to handle unseen words
quiz.why: Word-level tokenizers need an entry per word and turn new words into out-of-vocabulary tokens.

quiz.q: Why are per-token API prices of different models not directly comparable?
quiz.answer: Different tokenizers produce different token counts for the same text
distractors: All providers share the same tokenizer
quiz.why: The same text could be 120 tokens for one tokenizer and 165 for another.

quiz.q: What is true of the padding token <pad>?
quiz.answer: It aligns sequences in a batch and is ignored by the loss
distractors: It marks the end of generation
It separates user and assistant turns
It is predicted after every sentence
quiz.why: Padding exists only for batching; it is masked and never predicted by decoder-only models.

quiz.q: What happens if you replace a trained model's tokenizer with a different one?
quiz.answer: The text-to-ID mapping changes, so the model must be adapted or retrained
distractors: The model relearns the mapping automatically at inference
quiz.why: Tokenizer and model form a coupled system, and the output layer is sized to the vocabulary.

quiz.q: Why are raw token IDs not suitable as direct semantic input?
quiz.answer: They are arbitrary indices whose numeric distance has no linguistic meaning
distractors: They are too large to store
They change every time the model runs
quiz.why: ID 2317 is not closer in meaning to 2318 than to 57; embeddings provide meaningful geometry.

quiz.q: How many parameters does an embedding matrix with vocabulary size V and width d_model have?
quiz.answer: V · d_model
quiz.why: E has one row of length d_model per vocabulary entry, e.g. 100,000 × 4,096 ≈ 410 million.

quiz.q: What is the cosine similarity of two vectors pointing in exactly opposite directions?
quiz.why: Cosine similarity depends only on the angle; 180 degrees gives -1.

quiz.q: In trained embeddings, what does a large vector norm mainly indicate?
quiz.answer: The word is frequent or generic in the training data
distractors: The word has a very specific meaning
The word is an antonym of many words
quiz.why: Frequent words collect more gradient updates and longer vectors; direction carries meaning.

quiz.q: What does Word2Vec skip-gram predict?
quiz.answer: The surrounding context words from a centre word
distractors: The centre word from its context
quiz.why: Skip-gram takes the centre word as input and maximises the probability of its neighbours.

quiz.q: 'bank' appears in a finance sentence and a river sentence. What is true of its initial embedding?
quiz.answer: It is identical in both sentences
distractors: It is randomly re-sampled each time
It is zero until context is processed
quiz.why: The lookup is context-independent; contextual meaning is built later by attention layers.

quiz.q: What are logits?
quiz.answer: Raw, unnormalised scores, one for every vocabulary token
distractors: Probabilities that already sum to one
The embedding vectors of the input tokens
The IDs of the top-5 candidate tokens
quiz.why: Logits are scores; softmax turns them into probabilities and a decoding strategy then chooses a token.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a typical stopping condition for generation?
quiz.answer: The logit of the top token exceeds 1.0
distractors: A configured generation limit is reached
quiz.why: Generation stops on <eos>, length limits or other configured criteria, never on a logit threshold.

quiz.q: With a fixed context window, what is the effect of a longer prompt?
quiz.answer: Less room remains for generated tokens
distractors: Generated tokens no longer count toward the limit
quiz.why: Prompt and generated tokens share the same window: n_prompt + n_generated <= L.

quiz.q: What context window length did GPT-3 have?
quiz.answer: 2,048 tokens

quiz.q: Why is detokenization not simply joining token strings with spaces?
quiz.answer: Token boundaries do not match word boundaries; spaces are part of the tokens
distractors: Detokenization uses a different tokenizer than encoding
quiz.why: Tokens may be word pieces with leading spaces; decoding follows the tokenizer's byte rules.

quiz.q: During training, what is the predicted distribution compared against in the cross-entropy loss?
quiz.answer: A one-hot vector for the correct next token
quiz.why: The target is the input shifted by one; the loss is minus the log probability of the correct token.

quiz.q: Why do two occurrences of 'bank' in different sentences have the same vector right after the embedding lookup?
quiz.answer: The embedding lookup depends only on the token ID, not on context
distractors: Because the tokenizer merges both sentences
Because softmax normalizes them to the same value
Because the hidden state starts at zero
quiz.why: An embedding table maps each ID to one fixed row; context only enters through later layers.

quiz.q: In an RNN, which matrix carries information from the previous time step into the new hidden state?
quiz.answer: The recurrent hidden-to-hidden matrix W_hh
quiz.why: W_hh (H x H) multiplies h_(t-1), linking each step to the past.

quiz.q: What does the seq2seq decoder receive as its very first input token?
quiz.answer: <bos>, the beginning-of-sequence token
quiz.why: Generation starts from <bos>; afterwards each predicted token is fed back in.

quiz.q: In the example 'I love machine learning' -> 'Jag älskar maskininlärning', what does the length difference show?
quiz.answer: Input and output sequences in seq2seq can have different lengths
distractors: The decoder dropped a word by mistake
The encoder only reads three tokens
quiz.why: Four source tokens map to three target tokens plus <eos>; seq2seq decouples the lengths.

quiz.q: What is the core limitation of basic RNN seq2seq that motivates attention?
quiz.answer: All source information must pass through one fixed-size context vector
distractors: The encoder has no hidden state
quiz.why: The fixed vector cannot keep every detail of long inputs, and the decoder cannot look at individual encoder states.

quiz.q: Which scoring function does Luong-style attention typically use?
quiz.answer: A dot product between decoder state and encoder state
distractors: A learned additive network with tanh
The cosine of the token IDs
quiz.why: Luong attention scores with s . h; the additive tanh network is Bahdanau's version.

quiz.q: After softmax, what is true about the attention weights for one decoding step?
quiz.answer: They are positive and sum to 1
distractors: They sum to the number of source tokens
quiz.why: Softmax produces a probability distribution; uniform 0.25 was only an illustration.

quiz.q: How is the context vector c_t computed in attention-based seq2seq?
quiz.answer: As the attention-weighted sum of all encoder hidden states
distractors: As the final encoder state only
As the average of decoder states
As the embedding of the previous output token
quiz.why: c_t = sum of alpha_t,i h_i, recomputed at every step.

quiz.q: In the translation example, which source word gets the largest weight when 'älskar' is generated?
quiz.answer: love
quiz.why: At t = 2 attention concentrates on 'love', the source word that 'älskar' translates.

quiz.q: What does a bend away from the diagonal in a translation attention map indicate?
quiz.answer: The model learned a word reordering between the languages
distractors: That the decoder ignored the source
quiz.why: Non-monotonic alignment appears when the target language orders words differently.

quiz.q: What is the key architectural change the 2017 Transformer made compared with attention-based RNN seq2seq?
quiz.answer: It removed recurrence and relies entirely on attention
distractors: It replaced embeddings with one-hot vectors
It used a single fixed context vector
quiz.why: Without a recurrent chain, all known positions can be processed in parallel.

quiz.q: In self-attention, why must queries and keys have the same dimension d_k?
quiz.answer: Because they are compared with a dot product
distractors: Because values are summed with them
Because the vocabulary size equals d_k
quiz.why: A dot product is only defined for vectors of equal length; values may use a different size d_v.

quiz.q: Why are attention scores divided by sqrt(d_k)?
quiz.answer: To keep dot products from growing with dimension and making the softmax too peaked
distractors: To make the weights sum to one
To reduce the number of parameters
To block attention to future tokens
quiz.why: Large raw scores push softmax toward one-hot distributions; scaling keeps it smooth.

quiz.q: In the original Transformer with d_model = 512 and 8 heads, what is the per-head dimension d_k?
quiz.why: d_k = d_model / h = 512 / 8 = 64, and 8 x 64 concatenates back to 512.

quiz.q: What property holds for every row of a (softmax) attention matrix?
quiz.answer: Its weights sum to 1
distractors: It contains exactly one non-zero entry
quiz.why: Each row is a probability distribution over the keys for one query.

quiz.q: Which statement about attention head roles is correct?
quiz.answer: Roles emerge during training and may overlap or be uninterpretable
distractors: Each head is assigned a fixed linguistic role by design
quiz.why: Heads have separate learned projections; any role is an observed tendency, not a specification.

quiz.q: What happens to the outputs of unmasked self-attention without positional information if you shuffle the input tokens?
quiz.answer: The outputs are shuffled in the same way and otherwise unchanged
distractors: The model refuses to process the input
The outputs stay in the original order
quiz.why: Self-attention is permutation-equivariant: SelfAttn(PX) = P SelfAttn(X).

quiz.q: How are sinusoidal positional encodings combined with token embeddings in the original Transformer?
quiz.answer: They are added element-wise
distractors: They are concatenated after the last layer
They are multiplied with the attention weights
quiz.why: x_pos = e_token + PE(pos), both of size d_model.

quiz.q: Which dimensions of the sinusoidal encoding carry fine, local position information?
quiz.answer: The low dimension indices with high-frequency waves
distractors: The high dimension indices with slow waves
None - all dimensions change equally fast
quiz.why: Low indices oscillate quickly from position to position; high indices vary slowly and encode coarse position.

quiz.q: In the causal mask, what value is placed at positions j > i before softmax?
quiz.answer: Minus infinity
quiz.why: exp(minus infinity) = 0, so future tokens receive zero weight.

quiz.q: In the masked table for 'The bank raised interest rates', what is the row for 'The'?
quiz.why: The first token can only see itself, so all weight goes to position 1.

quiz.q: Why can a decoder Transformer train in parallel but must generate sequentially?
quiz.answer: In training the full sequence is known and masked; in inference future tokens do not exist yet
distractors: Training uses an RNN, inference uses attention
The mask is removed at inference
GPUs cannot run attention during inference
quiz.why: Masking simulates the prefix-only view during training; at inference each new token must be generated before the next.

quiz.q: In the original Transformer layer, what is the order of sublayers?
quiz.answer: Multi-head attention, Add & Norm, FFN, Add & Norm
quiz.why: The original design is Post-Norm: Add & Norm follows each of the two sublayers.

quiz.q: In Transformer Base (d_model = 512, d_ff = 2048), roughly how many weights does one FFN have compared with one attention block?
quiz.answer: About 2.10M vs about 1.05M, so roughly twice as many

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of a residual connection y = x + Sublayer(x)?
quiz.answer: The sublayer only learns an update and gradients flow directly backwards
distractors: It blocks attention to future tokens
It removes the need for embeddings
quiz.why: The identity path preserves information and gives gradients a shortcut to early layers.

quiz.q: Which model has d_model = 12288 and 96 layers?
quiz.answer: GPT-3 with 175B parameters
quiz.why: Transformer Base is 512 wide and Big is 1024 wide, both 6+6 layers; GPT-3 is 12288 wide with 96 layers.

quiz.q: When generating the next token after 'The cat sat on', which hidden state is projected by the LM head?
quiz.answer: Only the final state, the one for 'on'
distractors: The average of all four states
All four states, then summed logits
quiz.why: With causal attention the last state already contains all available context.

quiz.q: With V = 50,000 and d = 4,096, how many parameters does weight tying save?
quiz.answer: About 204.8M (from 409.6M down to 204.8M)
quiz.why: One V x d matrix (204.8M) is shared instead of learning two.

quiz.q: Why does Pre-LN allow much deeper Transformers than Post-LN?
quiz.answer: The residual skip path stays a pure identity, so gradients flow back without being reshaped by every norm.
distractors: It removes the residual connection entirely
It normalizes the gradients instead of the activations
It halves the number of parameters per layer
quiz.why: Post-LN puts LayerNorm on the residual path; Pre-LN only normalizes the sublayer input, leaving a direct gradient highway.

quiz.q: What does RMSNorm leave out compared with LayerNorm?
quiz.answer: Subtracting the mean (centering)
quiz.why: RMSNorm only divides by the root mean square and multiplies by gamma; it never re-centers the vector.

quiz.q: With RoPE, the attention score between a query at position m and a key at position n depends on...
quiz.answer: their content and the relative offset n - m
distractors: a lookup in a learned position table
a rotation applied to the value vectors
quiz.why: The two rotations combine into one rotation by n - m; values are not rotated at all.

quiz.q: A model has 32 query heads. How many KV heads do MHA, GQA with 8 groups and MQA have?
quiz.why: MHA keeps one K/V per query head, GQA one per group, MQA one shared by all.

quiz.q: What can a SwiGLU gate do that a sigmoid GLU gate cannot?
quiz.answer: Amplify features with gate values above 1
quiz.why: SiLU is unbounded above, while the sigmoid saturates below 1 and can only attenuate.

quiz.q: Why can the KV cache avoid recomputing earlier positions at each step?
quiz.answer: Causal masking keeps earlier keys and values unchanged when a new token is appended
distractors: The model stores only the last token
Attention is recomputed but averaged with a running mean
The prompt is split into non-overlapping blocks
quiz.why: Each token only attends to earlier ones, so appending a token never changes earlier representations, keys or values.

quiz.q: Which phase processes the whole prompt in parallel and produces the first output token?
quiz.answer: Prefill
quiz.why: Prefill builds the initial KV cache for every layer and its final position's logits pick the first token; decode then adds one token at a time.

quiz.q: A long output with a short prompt is dominated by which cost?
quiz.answer: The sequential decode steps
quiz.why: Total latency is roughly first-token time plus one decode step per token, so many output tokens make decode the dominant cost.

quiz.q: In the example model (32 layers, 32 query heads, head dimension 128, FP16), which factor do GQA's 8 KV heads and MQA's 1 KV head reduce?
quiz.answer: The number of KV heads, so the cache shrinks to 1/4 or 1/32 of full MHA
quiz.why: Cache size scales linearly with the KV-head count: MHA 16 GiB, GQA 4 GiB and MQA 512 MiB at 32,768 positions.

quiz.q: Does quantizing the model weights shrink the KV cache?
quiz.answer: No, because the cache stores activations and only KV-cache quantization reduces bytes per element
distractors: Yes, it shrinks the cache proportionally to the weights
Yes, but only for the value vectors
Only if the batch size is one
quiz.why: Weight quantization touches parameters; the cache holds keys and values, so it must be quantized separately.

quiz.q: What is the main goal of a sparse Mixture-of-Experts layer?
quiz.answer: To add trainable parameters without proportionally increasing the compute per token
distractors: To reduce the number of stored parameters
To remove the feed-forward layer entirely
quiz.why: Only a few experts run per token, so capacity grows while active compute stays low.

quiz.q: With router scores 2.0, 0.2, 1.0 and -0.5 and k equal to 2, which experts run and with what weights?
quiz.answer: Experts 1 and 3, with weights about 0.73 and 0.27
distractors: Experts 1 and 2, with weights about 0.9 and 0.1
All four experts, each weighted by its score
quiz.why: Top-k keeps the two largest scores, and the softmax is taken over only those two: exp(2.0) and exp(1.0) normalise to 0.73 and 0.27.

quiz.q: With 100M parameters per expert, what are the total and active expert parameters for 8 experts with 2 selected?
quiz.answer: 800M total and 200M active
quiz.why: Total is E * P_expert = 8 * 100M; active is k * P_expert = 2 * 100M.

quiz.q: Why is an auxiliary loss used when training a router?
quiz.answer: To encourage balanced expert usage so no expert is starved of training signals
distractors: To make the top-k selection differentiable
To reduce the number of experts stored
quiz.why: Without help routers can favour a few experts; the auxiliary loss levels the load, though perfect equality is not required.

quiz.q: What does quantizing the weights do for a MoE model's memory?
quiz.answer: It does not remove experts: weight memory does not drop, because all experts must stay stored
distractors: It deletes unselected experts at runtime
It cuts weight memory in half automatically
It only affects the KV cache
quiz.why: Sparse activation reduces compute, but every expert's weights remain in memory and available to be selected.

quiz.q: For one token, which experts receive a gradient during training?
quiz.answer: Only the selected experts, through their output vectors
distractors: Every expert, scaled by its router score
Only the router, not the experts
The unselected experts, through the top-k mask
quiz.why: Gradients reach selected experts via their outputs and the router via the softmax weights; unselected experts get none from that token.

quiz.q: In a state space model, what does the state vector represent?
quiz.answer: A fixed-size summary of everything seen so far, updated with each new token
distractors: A growing cache of every previous key and value
A copy of the current token only
The vocabulary logits of the last token
quiz.why: The SSM keeps one compact state whose size never depends on sequence length, unlike a KV cache.

quiz.q: What does Mamba add to a basic SSM?
quiz.answer: Input-dependent parameters, so the model can decide per token what to retain and write
distractors: A growing KV cache for exact lookups
quiz.why: Selectivity makes the update content-dependent, letting important tokens be remembered and filler fade.

quiz.q: In an LSTM, which gate decides how much previous cell memory to keep?
quiz.answer: The forget gate
quiz.why: The forget gate scales the old cell state, the input gate writes new content and the output gate exposes it.

quiz.q: How can Mamba and mLSTM be trained on a whole sequence in parallel despite being recurrent?
quiz.answer: Their updates depend only on the input tokens and can be combined algebraically
distractors: They discard the recurrent state during training
They replace recurrence with a KV cache
Their gates are independent of the inputs
quiz.why: Composable, input-only updates allow a parallel scan; generation is still sequential token by token.

quiz.q: What does Gated DeltaNet do that plain linear attention cannot?
quiz.answer: It forgets selectively and writes only the error (delta) between the new and predicted value
distractors: It stores every past key and value separately
It removes the feature map entirely
It grows a KV cache with context length
quiz.why: A retention gate plus an error-driven write correct stale associations instead of adding conflicting ones.

quiz.q: What is the prefill and per-token decode compute complexity of full attention in N context tokens?
quiz.answer: Quadratic prefill O(N^2) and linear decode O(N) per token
distractors: Linear prefill O(N) and constant decode O(1)
quiz.why: Full attention compares every prompt token with every other, and each decode step attends to all previous positions.

quiz.q: Which architecture class has linear prefill and constant per-token decode and state memory?
quiz.answer: Recurrent and linear-attention models such as Mamba, xLSTM and Gated DeltaNet
quiz.why: They keep a fixed-size state, so prefill is O(N) and decode and state are O(1).

quiz.q: Two models have the same Big-O. What can still make them run at different speeds?
quiz.answer: Kernel quality, memory bandwidth and GPU utilisation
distractors: Their parameter counts defined by Big-O
quiz.why: Big-O shows how cost scales, but real runtime depends on kernels, bandwidth and hardware utilisation.

quiz.q: Why is exact long-context recall harder for a fixed-state model than for full attention?
quiz.answer: It must squeeze every detail into one evolving state, so specific facts like a phone number can blur
distractors: It stores each past token in a separate cache slot
It cannot process prompts longer than one token
It uses more memory for older tokens
quiz.why: Full attention keeps token-specific keys and values for direct access, while a fixed state has limited capacity for exact detail.

quiz.q: For a service with many concurrent users and a memory limit, what does the lesson recommend?
quiz.answer: GQA or MQA, or fixed-state models, to reduce per-request memory
distractors: Full MHA with the largest context window
A looped model with many iterations
quiz.why: Fewer KV heads or a fixed state means each request needs less cache memory, which lets more users fit on one device.

quiz.q: FineWeb-Edu kept only documents with an educational score of at least 3. What happened to MMLU accuracy for a 1.71B model trained on 350B tokens?
quiz.answer: It rose from 33% to 37%
distractors: It stayed the same but training was faster
It dropped slightly because less data was used
quiz.why: Same model and token budget, better data: selecting educational text alone gave about 4 percentage points on MMLU.

quiz.q: Why is deduplication an important step in building a pretraining corpus?
quiz.answer: Repeated documents increase memorization and verbatim regurgitation and waste training compute
distractors: Deduplication is required to translate text into English
Duplicates cause the context window to overflow
quiz.why: Overrepresented copies push the model to memorize them; removing them reduces memorization and improves efficiency.

quiz.q: In a data mixture, what does upsampling a source mean?
quiz.answer: Drawing tokens from that source more often than its share of available data, possibly repeating it
distractors: Increasing the resolution of the source's text
Collecting more documents from that source with a crawler
Giving the source a larger learning rate
quiz.why: Mixture weights set token shares independent of availability; small valuable sources like code or math are sampled more often.

quiz.q: In the Phi-1 controlled experiment with a 350M model, what did adding synthetic textbook data change?
quiz.answer: The unit-test pass rate improved from 17.7% to 20.1%
distractors: The model grew from 350M to 1.3B parameters
The pass rate doubled from 20% to 40%
Training no longer needed real code at all
quiz.why: Synthetic textbooks added 2.4 percentage points without more parameters, showing data is a design lever, but not proving synthetic data always wins.

quiz.q: GPT-4 scores 85.5% on MMLU in English but 62.0% in Telugu. Which statement is most accurate?
quiz.answer: Data imbalance is a likely cause, but the evaluation alone does not prove the cause
distractors: Telugu questions were harder by design
It proves the tokenizer is the only cause
The model was never trained on any non-English text
quiz.why: Plausible causes include training-data imbalance, tokenization efficiency and translation effects; a measured disparity does not identify which one dominates.

quiz.q: Roughly how large was the August 2025 Common Crawl archive?
quiz.answer: About 2.44 billion web pages
quiz.why: The CC-MAIN-2025-33 crawl contained around 2.44 billion pages, roughly 47 TB.

quiz.q: The model assigns probability 0.10 to the correct next token. What is the cross-entropy loss at that position?
quiz.answer: About 2.30, since -ln(0.10) ≈ 2.30
distractors: Zero, because the model was confident
quiz.why: Cross-entropy is the negative log of the target probability: a low probability gives a large loss.

quiz.q: Using the ~6 FLOPs per parameter per token rule, how many FLOPs does one step of a 7B model with 2,048 tokens per step need?
quiz.answer: About 8.6e13 FLOPs
quiz.why: 6 * 7e9 * 2048 ≈ 8.6e13; a 70B model would be about ten times higher, near 8.6e14.

quiz.q: Why does LLM training begin with a linear learning-rate warm-up?
quiz.answer: Adam's moment estimates are still unreliable early, so large steps could destabilize training
distractors: To increase the effective batch size
To let the tokenizer adapt to the data
Because the FLOP count is unknown at the start
quiz.why: Warm-up ramps the rate from near zero so the optimizer can build trustworthy mean and variance estimates before taking big steps.

quiz.q: How do batch sizes affect gradient estimates in pretraining?
quiz.answer: Small batches give noisy gradients; large batches give smoother gradients and better hardware efficiency
distractors: Small batches always converge faster to lower loss
Batch size does not affect gradient noise
Large batches remove the need for an optimizer
quiz.why: A larger batch averages more examples, reducing gradient noise, though it does not automatically speed up convergence.

quiz.q: Which numbers describe the NVIDIA H100 used for LLM training?
quiz.answer: 80 GB HBM3 memory, 3.35 TB/s bandwidth, up to 700 W
quiz.why: The H100 SXM has 80 GB HBM3, 3.35 TB/s memory bandwidth, NVLink up to 900 GB/s and up to 700 W.

quiz.q: A batch has 2,048 token sequences of length 4,096. Roughly how many tokens does one optimizer step process?
quiz.answer: About 8.4 million tokens
quiz.why: Tokens per batch = B * L = 2,048 * 4,096 ≈ 8.4 million.

quiz.q: Why is BF16 the standard format for LLM training rather than FP16?
quiz.answer: BF16 keeps FP32's 8 exponent bits, giving a wide range at 16-bit cost, while FP16's smaller range can overflow
distractors: BF16 has more fraction bits than FP32
BF16 needs loss scaling but FP16 does not
BF16 uses 24 exponent bits for extra precision
